**﴿The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾** (Az-Zumar: 1)

There is a difference between *nuzul* (نزول), *inzal* (إنزال) and *tanzil* (تنزيل). *Nuzul* is the event of something coming down from a higher place to a lower one. *Inzal* indicates that the one who sends down is higher than the one to whom it is sent down. *Tanzil* indicates descent in stages, according to circumstances.

So Allah's words **﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾** (Al-Qadr: 1) mean: We sent it down all at once at the beginning of the mission of Muhammad, so that the Qur'an could begin its task in existence. Then it was sent down in parts (*munajjaman*), as needed.

He, the Exalted, says: **﴿And with the truth We have sent it down, and with the truth it has descended. And We have not sent you, [O Muhammad], except as a bringer of good tidings and a warner.﴾** (Al-Isra': 105)

That is: We sent it down with the truth from the beginning, and it has remained upon the truth. No one has been able to change or corrupt it, because it is truth.

This root, *nazala*, *nazzala* or *anzala*, all indicate the exalted position of the one who sends down and the nearness of the one to whom it is sent. They also indicate that the honour of what is sent down derives from the honour of the one who sent it. Furthermore, they indicate that the One who sends down the straight way to the creature wishes to honour him and to elevate him. Thus *inzal* indicates the honour and high station of the one who sends down, the honour of what is sent down, and the honour of the one whom Allah has chosen and made fit to receive this good.

Among this is His saying concerning the community of Muhammad: **﴿You are the best nation produced for mankind﴾** (Al 'Imran: 110)...

And *al-Kitab* (الكتاب) means the Qur'an. He says "the Book" at one time and "the Qur'an" at another, which shows that it takes both descriptions together. It is a *kitab* in the sense of something recorded and written, which cannot be denied, and it is a *Qur'an* in the sense of something recited. It is recorded in lines and preserved in hearts, and this will be a proof against us.

We know the precision that the Companions followed in collecting the Qur'an from the memories of those who had memorised it. They would not write down a verse until two of the memorisers had recited it and agreed on its correctness. Likewise, two witnesses would attest to its correctness after it was written. This precision demonstrates the grounds for His saying: **﴿Indeed, We have sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian.﴾** (Al-Hijr: 9)

The word *al-Kitab*, with the definite article *al-*, indicates that it is the complete Book among books, and this word refers to nothing but the Noble Qur'an.

His saying **﴿from Allah﴾** (Az-Zumar: 1) shows that the descent is from the higher to the lower. But why did He say "from Allah" and not "from the Lord (*Rabb*)"? Because this Book came with a method of upbringing (*tarbiyah*), and the Lord (*Rabb*) is the one who takes charge of creation and of nurturing. It has been said: because lordship (*rububiyyah*) is a gift that includes everyone, believer and disbeliever, obedient and disobedient. The Lord created all of creation, material creation, and sustained everyone, so all are equal in the gift of lordship.

As for the method that the Book was sent down with, it is a method of faith, morality and worship, which is a gift of divinity (*uluhiyyah*), not a gift of lordship. Therefore He said of the Book: **﴿from Allah﴾** (Az-Zumar: 1).

*Allah* is a proper name (*'alam*) for the Necessarily Existent. The Most Beautiful Names (*al-asma' al-husna*) are descriptions that have reached the highest degree of greatness, because they belong to Allah, the Exalted, and have come to predominate, so they became names. He, the Exalted, says: **﴿And to Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names, so invoke Him by them﴾** (Al-A'raf: 180). The word that comprises all of them is the name *Allah*. When you say "Allah," it is as if you have called upon Allah by all His Most Beautiful Names. Therefore we were commanded to begin every action with "In the name of Allah."

An action requires strength, knowledge, wisdom, might, and so on. If you were about to undertake an action that requires twenty attributes, for example, would you say "In the name of the Strong, in the name of the Knowing, in the name of the Wise..."? No, because you are able to gather all these attributes in your saying "In the name of Allah," since the word *Allah* is the all-comprehensive word for every attribute of perfection, and it suits everything the action requires and everything connected with the deed, whether you know it or not.

Therefore they said: beware of leaving this word out at the beginning of an action...

So, He, glory be to Him, said: **﴿The revelation of the Book is from Allah﴾** (Az-Zumar: 1), because the Book was sent down with a method and values. He did not say "from the Lord," because *Rabb* is a description specific to matter and form.

As for His saying **﴿the Mighty, the Wise﴾** (Az-Zumar: 1), *al-'Aziz* means the One who is free from need of creation, whose obedience does not benefit Him and whose disobedience does not harm Him. This description came after **﴿The revelation of the Book is from Allah﴾** for a reason. It is as if the Truth, glory be to Him, is saying to us: know that I have freely given this method that I have sent down to you, and I intend by it your happiness in this world and your bliss in the Hereafter. As for your obedience to My method, it adds nothing to My dominion, because I am free from need of you. I am the Mighty, independent of My creation...

So, say "In the name of Allah," and know that He is Mighty above this... The Truth, glory be to Him, is the Mighty who overcomes and is not overcome. He bestows this attribute upon whoever believes in Him, so the believer has might from the might of Allah. As for the one who does not believe, he seeks might through sin, through arrogance without any basis... Although the Truth, glory be to Him, is *al-'Aziz*, the one who overcomes and is not overcome, He is also **﴿al-Hakim﴾**, that is, the One who places things in their proper places. From this wisdom is that He does not make the believer constantly mighty, nor constantly humble, nor constantly merciful, nor constantly stern. Rather, he responds to the events of faith, as He, glory be to Him, said: **﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him are forceful against the disbelievers and merciful among themselves﴾** (Al-Fath: 29), and He said: **﴿humble towards the believers, mighty over the disbelievers﴾** (Al-Ma'idah: 54).

Although these are dispositions in the self, they are moderated by the method of the One who created them. If the situation calls for mercy, the believer is merciful; if the situation calls for firmness, the believer is firm. This is a manifestation of the wisdom of the Creator, glory be to Him. If you say: these are dispositions, yes, they are dispositions, but they are moderated by the method of the One who created them.

The truth is the established matter that the changing circumstances of time cannot come and overturn. Since the truth is firm and does not change, let not the rise of falsehood deceive you, even if it rises for a day of the days; for the rise of falsehood is part of the firmness of the truth. When falsehood rises, it bites people, creatures suffer from it, and they are scorched by its fire, and at that point they long for the truth and yearn for it.

So falsehood is like a soldier from among the soldiers of the truth, and disbelief is like a soldier from among the soldiers of faith. God, exalted is He, never leaves the truth unprotected, but He leaves it for a period until falsehood rises over it, in order to test people's zeal for it. If they do not show zeal for it, He Himself becomes zealous for it.

﴿So worship God﴾: meaning, since We have sent down to you the Book with the truth, look at what is in the Book. In it is a method: do this and do not do that. In it is an obligation upon the limbs (al-takleef, "religious obligation"), and the work must necessarily be preceded by the heart's conviction in the one who imposes the obligation and by faith in him.

So when you stand before a difficult matter that you cannot think through, or a decision you must take, you go to someone known for wisdom, knowledge and good judgment, so that he may think for you and help you with your affair. Such a man you trust, and you entrust to him the reins of your affair, because his opinion will set you right.

Thus: before acting on "do" and "do not do," it is necessary that you trust and be certain of the one who imposed the obligation, and this is the faith that ought to precede the action. Therefore we say: there is no benefit in faith without action, nor in action without faith. Consider the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿The Bedouins say: "We have believed." Say: "You have not believed; rather say, 'We have submitted,' for faith has not yet entered your hearts."﴾ [al-Hujurat: 14].

Therefore God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So worship God, sincere to Him in religion﴾. The condition of worship is sincerity (ikhlas), and worship means the worshipper's obedience to the commands and prohibitions of the one worshipped. This definition of the meaning of worship nullifies the worship of everything other than God, exalted is He. Those who worshipped other than God, whether the sun, the moon, the stars, trees or stones, worshipped gods, as they claim, without a method and without obligations.

Thus the word "worship" used here for them is mistaken and false. What did these gods say to them? What did they command them, and what did they forbid them? What did these gods prepare for whoever worshipped them, and what did they prepare for whoever disbelieved in them? The first thing that nullifies the worship of other than God is that these gods have no method and no obligations.

As for those who said: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to God in closeness﴾ [al-Zumar: 3], God, glorified is He, forbade this closeness, and forbade that there be between Him and His servants an intermediary or a means...

The meaning of ﴿sincere to Him in religion﴾ is: make the religion purely for the sake of God's countenance, and avoid showing off (riya'), because the one you show off to cannot own for you any reward for the deed. The one who shows off, for example, in his charity, benefits the needy with the charity, but he himself gains nothing from it, because God leaves him to take his reward from the one he showed off to, and a servant like you owns nothing for you.

There is a difference in meaning between mukhlis (with a kasra on the lam, "one who is sincere") and mukhlas (with a fatha on the lam, "one who has been purified"): the mukhlas is the one whose sincerity precedes God's bestowal upon him, so he becomes sincere; whereas the mukhlis reaches, through the bestowal of his sincerity, God's bestowal. We have said elsewhere: among people is one who reaches God's honour through obedience to God, meaning he persists in obedience and continually knocks at the door until it is opened to him.

Another reaches obedience to God through God's honour, meaning his Lord chooses him for obedience and snatches him from the creatures, or from disobedience, to obedience...

ThenHe, glory be to Him, says: "Surely to God belongs pure religion" (ألا لله الدين الخالص), after the Truth, glory be to Him, had addressed His Prophet with the words: "So worship God, making your religion sincerely His" [al-Zumar: 2]. He, glory be to Him, wished to alert minds to the importance of sincerity to God, the Exalted, and so He brought this particle indicating the opening of speech: "Surely" (ألا).

This is a style that the Arab follows in his speech, because the speaker is master of himself: he speaks whenever he wishes, he is aware of what he says, and he has a choice in what he says. As for the listener, he has no choice; he may be occupied and so miss part of what is said. Therefore the speaker must rouse him from his heedlessness and prepare him to listen, especially if the speech is important or precious, of which nothing should escape you. Therefore He, glory be to Him, said: "Surely to God belongs pure religion" [al-Zumar: 3].

We also notice here the style of restriction (qasr) in the fronting of the prepositional phrase "to God" (لله) [al-Zumar: 3] before the subject "pure religion" (الدين الخالص). He did not say "pure religion belongs to God," because that could allow one to say "and to other than Him." But His words "to God belongs pure religion" [al-Zumar: 3], meaning: to Him alone, restrict the sincerity of religion to God, the Exalted, to the exclusion of others. You say: "This wealth is for Zayd" and "For Zayd is this wealth."

But why is it "to God belongs pure religion"? They said: because religion (al-din) is the Law of God, which He has legislated, and it is He, glory be to Him, who rewards for it. So beware, then, lest your action according to God's method be intended for other than God, for other than God has not legislated it for you, and cannot give you the reward for the deed. It is as though God, the Exalted, wants to fortify the movement of a human being in everything, such that all his movements return to him with good; therefore He guided him to the path that leads him to good, which is the path of sincerely devoting worship to God alone.

Then He mentions, in contrast to sincere worship of God, He says: "And those who take protectors other than Him [say]: 'We only serve them so that they may bring us near to God in closeness'" [al-Zumar: 3]. They speak and justify their stance when it becomes clear to them that their worship of what is other than God is false, and when it is said to them that these deities neither see, nor hear, nor harm, nor benefit; and when the noose tightens upon them, they say: "We do not worship them except that they may bring us near to God in closeness."

Whatever brings you near to God must necessarily be witnessed as subordinate to God, the Exalted, whereas these deities you worship are not witnessed as subordinate to God, the Exalted; rather they are the product of your own making and the work of your hands. If the wind knocks it down, you set it up in its place, and if its arm is broken, you repair it.

So: your worship of them is void, and you are liars in this worship. "Surely God will judge between them concerning that wherein they differ" [al-Zumar: 3]. The word "judgment" belongs to God, a word that inspires awe, because the judgment of God is the Truth that favours no one. The believer, when he hears this word, is reassured, because there will come a day when judgment belongs to none but God, as He, glory be to Him, said: "Judgment belongs only to God" (إن الحكم إلا لله), i.e., to God alone and not to another. Therefore you do not say to your adversary: "I have made God judge between me and you" unless you are confident that the truth is with you...

Then, surely God's judgment will come at a time when there is no judgment except God's: "Judgment belongs only to God" [al-An'am: 57].

Then He, glory be to Him, says: "Surely God does not guide one who is a liar, a disbeliever" [al-Zumar: 3]. Indeed, God does not guide him, because the lying disbeliever is not fit to receive the gift of guidance; for God, the Exalted, guided all of them with the guidance of indication and direction, and whoever of them believes, He increases him in the guidance of help and success. He, glory be to Him, said: "And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and gives them their piety" [Muhammad: 17].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 39, verse 4:

This verse speaks of another kind of shirk. These people did not worship idols, the sun, or the moon. Rather, they took other things which they see as having a connection with Allah the Exalted, as we say "from his blessing" (min rayhatihi). They saw that this was lighter and easier than worshipping idols. These are like those who said "Uzair is the son of Allah," and those who said "the Messiah is the son of Allah," or "the angels are the daughters of Allah," etc. So Allah refuted them:

﴿Had Allah wished to take a son, He would have chosen whom He willed from what He creates.﴾ [Az-Zumar: 4] Meaning: this is a matter in which you have no say and no choice. Do not choose for Allah a son, for if Allah the Exalted had wished that, on supposition, He would have chosen from His creation whom He willed, not whom you choose.

Therefore the Truth, glorified is He, addressed His Prophet ﷺ with His saying: ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers.﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 81] That is: if it were by His choice and He announced it, ﴿then I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 81], meaning: the first of those who affirm and believe in it. So it is "upon the eye and the head" (i.e., gladly accepted). But this is a matter which Allah did not report, and He has negated it from Himself, glorified is He.

It has been related in a hadith: So sonship is not for Allah the Exalted. Even in the sonship of the Messengers, Allah did not make it a sonship of blood or of bodies, but a sonship of religion. The clearest example of this is our master Noah, peace be upon him, and his son.

When the son refused and disobeyed his father's command, the father became certain that he was among the perished, and he called upon Allah: ﴿He said: My Lord, my son is of my family, and surely Your promise is true, and You are the most just of judges.﴾ [Hud: 45] But Allah corrected his understanding of sonship, so He said, glorified is He: ﴿He said: O Noah, he is not of your family; indeed, he is one whose deed is other than righteous.﴾ [Hud: 46] So our master Noah thought that sonship meant sonship by lineage, but the sonship of the prophets is sonship of following (ittiba').

The particle (law) in ﴿Had Allah wished to take a son﴾ [Az-Zumar: 4] is a particle of prohibition due to prohibition (imtina' li-imtina'), and it is one of the conditional particles, indicating that the consequent is prevented because the condition is prevented. So the Truth, glorified is He, did not take a son because He did not will it; and if He had willed it, what He willed would have been.

In another place, the Truth, glorified is He, debates the proponents of this fabrication, saying to them by way of logic: ﴿How can He have a son when He has no consort?﴾ [Al-An'am: 101].

Then why is a son taken? A son is taken to be a source of strength for his father or an extension of him after his death. But the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, is the Self-Sufficient, the Mighty, free from His creation, and He is the Everlasting, the Remaining. So why would a son be taken? As for those who attributed a son to Allah the Exalted in the later ages of religions, like those who said "the Messiah is the son of Allah": was Allah, from the time He created this universe, without a son until Jesus came, and then Allah took him as a son?

And after Jesus was taken out of existence, did Allah the Exalted remain thus (like a lone, cut-off branch from a tree) without a son? How can this claim be valid for you? It is a matter that is never valid with respect to Allah the Exalted, for Allah has no need of a source of strength, nor does He need the help of a son, because Allah the Exalted created all creation from A to Z, created it by His complete power, with the attributes of perfection in Him, so creation added to Him nothing, nor any attribute that He did not previously have.

Therefore some of the people of ecstatic utterance (ahl al-shath) say concerning this verse: ﴿Had Allah wished to take a son, He would have chosen whom He willed from what He creates﴾ [Az-Zumar: 4], saying: "If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be more entitled to be His son, because I am the first of the worshippers."

Then the Truth, glorified is He, concludes this verse with what declares Allah far above this fabrication: ﴿Glory be to Him! He is Allah﴾ [Az-Zumar: 4]. Meaning: glorify Him and declare Him free of this matter, for it does not befit Him, glorified is He, and declare Him free of resembling anything of His creation. Even if you face a matter your intellect does not grasp, say "Subhan Allah (Glory be to Allah)," as Allah said: ﴿Glory be to He who created all the pairs﴾ [Ya-Sin: 36].

And He said: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾ [Ar-Rum: 17].

And He said: ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night﴾ [Al-Isra': 1].

So the Truth, glorified is He, in such situations teaches us to declare Allah free of such things, because the intellect will stand bewildered before these events. But the event here is attributed to Allah, so there is no wonder, for the time of an event is inversely proportional to the active power: whenever the power increases, the time decreases; if you attribute the act to the power of powers, you find no time at all.

So then: declare Allah free of taking a son, for He is ﴿Allah﴾ [Az-Zumar: 4], who possesses all attributes of perfection, ﴿the One﴾, with none besides Him, ﴿the Subduer﴾, meaning: who needs no source of strength and needs no helper.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 39, verse 5:

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾ [al-Zumar: 5]. That is, He did not create them in vain; rather He created them with truth. And truth, as we have said, is the thing that is established and does not change, as He, glorified is He, said in another verse: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ [al-Dukhan: 38].

Rather, Allah created them with truth, with wisdom, with precise calculation and wondrous engineering, so that they might fulfil the mission that the Creator, glorified is He, intended for them. The proof is that they have not ceased, since Allah created them, to fulfil their mission without any defect in them or disagreement among their parts.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night﴾ [al-Zumar: 5]. You say "kawwartu al-'amamah" (I wound the turban), meaning I wrapped it around my head, so it became like a round ball (kurrah), wound up. In wrapping a turban, one layer covers the layer beneath it. Likewise the night and the day: a part of the night covers a part of the day so the night increases, or a part of the day covers a part of the night so the day increases.

This is the reality of night and day. Do the night and the day divide the twenty-four hours equally, each one twelve hours?

No. Rather, the night increases and the day decreases in the winter season, and the day increases and the night decreases in the summer season.

This indicates that the universe is not governed by rigid mechanical laws as they claim, but is governed by the power and wisdom of the Creator, glorified is He.

If you reflect on the length of the night in winter and its shortness in summer, you will find that the affairs of the universe do not proceed in this manner by chance; rather, every movement in it has a wisdom. When the day is short in winter, the worker needs to exert himself to finish his task in this short time, so he tires and exhausts himself.

And it is wise that we give him a longer period in which he rests from the fatigue of the day, and the period of rest must necessarily be proportionate to the period of effort expended.

As for the summer season, the day lengthens and the work is distributed over this long time, so a person performs his task with the least exertion, in addition to his rest during the time of qaylulah (midday rest). Thus he does not need a long night for rest, and therefore the night of summer comes short. So: the Creator, glorified is He, wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night, for a wisdom in the movement of life.

In another place the Qur'an expressed this meaning by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾ [Fatir: 13], meaning: He makes each of them enter into the other. Therefore the night and the day are equal only for a short period of the year that the movement between them requires.

We also understand from His saying, exalted is He, "yukawwiru" (wraps), that the earth is spherical, because the night and the day are phenomena that occur on the surface of the earth, and science has established this fact through the images that they have taken of the earth from space. And Allah has spoken truly: ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth﴾ [Fussilat: 53].

And His saying: ﴿And He subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term﴾ [al-Zumar: 5].

The term (ajal) is the Day of Resurrection. The True One, glorified is He, reassures people that the sun and the moon are two signs of Allah, exalted is He, remaining and eternal for as long as this world remains and endures, until they both end with it. Nevertheless, each of them subsists in its own essence by the power of its Creator; it does not need fuel, it does not need maintenance, nor a calibration piece... etc.

﴿Unquestionably, He is the Mighty, the Forgiving﴾ [al-Zumar: 5]. We have said that "alā" (unquestionably) is an opening particle that serves to alert the listener to what follows, as if Allah, exalted is He, is saying: I have created for you this precise and wondrous universe, and I have provided for you the means of your life, and I am the Self-Sufficient, free of need of you, the Mighty who overcomes and is not overcome, who needs no one. But what is the fitting relation of "al-Ghaffar" (the Forgiving) here?

They said: Because Allah has bestowed favour upon His creation through these signs, the sun, the moon, the night and the day, and has given them the means of their life; and yet He does not hold their sins and their shortcomings in regard to His right against them, because He is al-Ghaffar, and He pardons much.

This meaning was clarified by the True One, glorified is He, in another place, and when we reflect upon it we find in it something marvellous. It is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And if you should count the favour of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾ [Ibrahim: 34]. This phrase occurs in two places with one opening and different endings. The first: ﴿And if you should count the favour of Allah, you could not enumerate it. Indeed, mankind is {very} wrongdoing and ungrateful﴾ [Ibrahim: 34].

And the second: ﴿And if you should count the favour of Allah, you could not enumerate it. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nahl: 18].

First: what draws our attention here, in the matter of counting the favour of Allah, is the use of "in" (if), which indicates doubt, because counting the favour of Allah is a matter that will never be and never occurs; for the undertaking to count a thing arises from the possibility of doing so and the capacity for it. As for the favour of Allah, even with the advance of the science of statistics and its entry into all fields, the favour of Allah is beyond the expectation of counting because of its abundance, just as we never think of counting the sand of the desert, for example.

So the meaning of ﴿And if you should count﴾ [Ibrahim: 34] is: supposing that you were to undertake to count it, ﴿you could not enumerate it﴾ [Ibrahim: 34].

Second: the word "ni'mah" (favour) came in this singular form, whereas counting applies only to a plurality that has parts that can be counted: one, two, three, four, etc. So how can a favour be counted when it is one? They said: Yes, in its outward appearance it is one favour, but within it are hidden many favours when you reflect upon it. The apple, for example, appears outwardly to be one favour, but when you dissect it you find in it colour, shape, taste, flavour, constituent elements and various nutritional substances, all of them favours from Allah.

Third: when you reflect upon the ending of the two verses, which is our concern in this discussion, you find in the first verse ﴿Indeed, mankind is {very} wrongdoing and ungrateful﴾ [Ibrahim: 34], meaning: one who denies the favour of Allah, rejects it, is heedless of it, and falls short in thanking for it. It therefore speaks of the condition of the human being toward the Benefactor: how he met the favour with ingratitude. Were the Benefactor to repay him according to what he deserves, He would deprive him of the favour. But the ending of the other verse comes: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nahl: 18], meaning: He forgives you your denial of the favour and your ingratitude for the kindness; then, after forgiveness, mercy.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 39, verse 6:

The verse clarifies the nature of the creation of man, whom He willed to be His vicegerent (khalifah) on earth. He says: ﴿He created you from a single soul﴾, namely Adam, peace be upon him. ﴿Then He made from it its mate﴾, that is, Eve. From the two of them came the offspring, and procreation began.

Since Allah the Exalted created this creature to be a vicegerent who cultivates the earth, it is necessary that they be of one kind, so that affinity and harmony may be realised among them and the movement of life may unite them.

For if this vicegerent were of multiple kinds, a group of humans, for example, another of jinn, and another of animals, life would not be upright for them, and their movement would not support one another. Therefore, within a single kind, affection, affinity, love and harmony among its members are available, because every kind has its own law (qanun), its own system, its own meeting-points and its own way of association. Had man been created from different kinds, it would have been impossible for him to achieve concord, unity of movement and comfort in livelihood.

Also, the Creator, glorified is He, created man from a single kind in order to establish equality in origin, so that no one has a merit over another on the ground that he was created from a superior kind. Rather, preference and merit are by the measure of this creature's conformity with the method of Allah. This matter was clarified by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the hadith: "No Arab has any virtue over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab, except by piety (taqwa)."

The Truth, glorified is He, says: ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13], meaning: no one among you has a virtue over another except by his goodness in what he presents before his Lord. Colours and shapes come in different forms to suit the environment of livelihood: the inhabitants of hot environments, for example, tend toward darkness, and those of cold environments toward fairness. The same applies to the difference of tongues according to environments. As for the origin, we are all traced back to Adam, and Adam was created from clay, and his descendants were created after him through multiplication.

Even concerning the Messenger, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128], meaning: he is not a stranger to you, and is not of a kind other than your kind. Thus He did not send an angel, for example, although angels are of higher rank, because an angel-messenger does not realise the exemplary model and pattern intended in a Messenger. Likewise He did not come as a Persian or a Roman whose tongue differs from your tongue; rather he came as an Arab, from the middle of you and from your greatest tribes.

Thus all of mankind in this universe returns to a single soul, which is Adam, peace be upon him, and the Truth, glorified is He, has made clear to us how Adam was created in the known form. He, glorified is He, said: ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, fall down before him in prostration﴾ [al-Hijr: 29]...

Then He, exalted is He, says, enumerating some of His blessings upon His creatures: ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of cattle﴾. We have said at the beginning of this surah that sending down (inzal) is not viewed only in terms of height, as in the sending down of the method and values; it is also viewed in terms of the One who sends down, glorified is He. Sending down may mean bringing into existence, and cattle are among the blessings present on earth, yet they are from whom? From Allah. So it is as if He sent them down. The sending down here is matched by the preposition ﴿for you﴾ (lakum) and not "upon you" (alaykum), because cattle are something separate from man.

The details of these eight are given in Surat al-An'am. Although Allah's blessings upon us are many, He singled out cattle here in particular, because they are the kind closest to man in terms of creation; after them come plants, then inanimate matter. As for the word zawj (pair): some think it means two together, but this is an error, because zawj means one together with its like. Among its uses is His saying: ﴿And of everything We created pairs﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 49]. Similar to it is the word tawam (twin).

As for His saying: ﴿He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation, in three darknesses﴾, the meaning of ﴿creation after creation﴾ is an explanation of the stages of creation through which the foetus passes in its mother's womb. It moves about in her belly between a despicable fluid, settling in the womb as a nutfah (drop), then an 'alaqah (clinging clot), then a mudghah (lump of flesh), then bones are formed from it, then it clothes the bones with flesh. These are the stages of creation intended in His saying: ﴿creation after creation﴾.

He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We certainly created man from an extract of clay. Then We made him a drop in a firm place of storage. Then We made the drop into a clinging clot, then We made the clot into a lump, then We made the lump into bones, then We clothed the bones with flesh; then We produced him as another creation. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12-14].

These are the stages through which man passes from the moment he reaches the mother's womb. This means that there is a stage preceding these stages, namely the stage of the meeting of the male element with the female element, that is, the meeting of the sperm with the ovum and its fertilisation; for only a fertilised ovum, into which the microbe of maleness has entered, reaches the womb.

In Surat al-Hajj He, glorified is He, made clear that the lump is of two kinds, formed and unformed: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then indeed, We created you from dust, then from a drop, then from a clinging clot, then from a lump of flesh, formed and unformed, that We may make clear to you. And We settle in the wombs whom We will for a specified term﴾ [al-Hajj: 5].

The formed lump is the part from which the organs and limbs are formed, while the unformed lump is the part which remains in the body without being formed, so that it stays as a reserve for the body... or a maintenance pharmacy. When damage occurs in the body, the unformed lump repairs it, as we see for example in wounds: after a period the wound heals, and its tissues are built up until it returns to what it was. From where? From the unformed lump...

So His saying ﴿He creates you in the wombs of your mothers﴾ refers to the second creation. The first creation was the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, from dust, and Allah informed us of it because no one witnessed it, as He said: ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor their own creation, nor would I have taken misguiding ones as assistants﴾ [al-Kahf: 51].

If someone appears to us saying that man's origin is an ape that evolved into a human, we know that he is among the misguiders about whom Allah has informed us, and it is necessary that we know his falsehood. The refutation of this nonsense is easy: if man evolved from an ape, why did the rest of the apes not evolve? And why, throughout all of history, have we never seen an ape evolve and rise even to something approaching a human?

Thus this is a lie and falsehood, because the Creator, glorified is He, created all kinds and made of each two spouses, so that reproduction is accomplished and separation is effected. He said: ﴿And of everything We created pairs, that perhaps you may remember﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 49].

His saying, glorified is He, ﴿in three darknesses﴾ is an explanation of the firm place of storage in which man settles in his mother's womb. He said: ﴿So We placed him in a firm place of storage, for a known period﴾ [al-Mursalat: 21-22]. The makin (firm) is that which is settled in a place; the mother's belly is a place, and the foetus in the belly is makin.

When the scholars spoke about the meaning of the three darknesses, they said: they are the darkness of the belly, the darkness of the womb, and the darkness of the placenta.

From the word "darkness" we understand several matters.

Firstly: darkness means the absence of light, and it is associated with the night.

Secondly: the night is always moister than the day, because in the day there is the heat of the sun and the heat of breaths arising from movement, whereas breaths at night are calm, because they serve merely to preserve life, and do not arise from the movement of work and exertion.

Thirdly: in darkness there is also stillness and calm, which is not available in the day.

Thus in darkness there is absence of light, there is coolness, and there is stillness. These three matters are necessary for the growth of the foetus and the formation of its organs in its mother's belly, because in its mother's belly it is a weak creation whose organs and limbs are not complete; it cannot bear heat, nor bear light, nor bear disturbing sounds. Therefore the Creator, glorified is He, provided for it insulators that protect it from these things. Hence He said: ﴿in three darknesses﴾.

The closer to correctness is that these three darknesses are in the womb, and that the darkness of the belly is not among them; for the Truth, glorified is He, speaks to us about the firm place of storage specific to the foetus, saying: ﴿in the wombs of your mothers﴾ as an explanation of the general container in which the specific container of the foetus, which is the womb, lies. The belly is a large container that contains the womb, the intestines, the stomach, the liver, the spleen, the pancreas, and so on. Therefore He specified the particular container of the foetus, saying after it: ﴿in three darknesses﴾.

Thus the three darknesses are insulations and membranes that protect the child, and all of them are inside the womb. If a mature, fully developed human is disturbed by sounds, which may even damage his eardrum, and is harmed by high lights, so that his sight cannot withstand them, can the foetus bear such things while its organs are not yet complete?

It is well known that a child is born with a thin skin that cannot bear heat, and is born with some organs and limbs not yet complete: the nervous system, for example, is not complete until several years have passed; the mental faculty does not mature until after the age of puberty; and the eye does not perform its function of sight until after three days.

The foetus therefore needs protection; that is why Allah placed it in a container within a container within a container, just as you might place your important papers in a file, the file in a safe, and the safe in a room. His saying ﴿in﴾ is thus a proof of the care given to this creature and the provision of the surrounding conditions suited to it.

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿That is Allah, your Lord; to Him belongs sovereignty﴾ [al-Zumar: 6]. The phrase ﴿That﴾ (dhalikum) is composed of the demonstrative (dha) and the pronoun of the addressees, and the indication here is to the Truth, blessed and exalted is He...

This indication to the Truth, glorified is He, came after He had spoken of some of His secrets in the creation of man, and of the three darknesses in the mother's womb, all of which belong to the domain of creation, nurturing and the first formation of man. This matter is fitted by the attribute of lordship (rububiyyah), which undertakes creation and nurture; the Lord is the Creator and the Nurturer. As for the word Allah, it pertains to divinity (uluhiyyah), and divinity entails obligation (taklif), because Allah means the One worshipped through obedience to His commands and avoidance of His prohibitions. The foetus in its mother's belly is far from the matter of obligation. So why did He choose here, in this context, the term divinity (Allah), saying: ﴿That is Allah, your Lord﴾?

And why did He not say: "That is your Lord, Allah," as some orientalists say?

They said: so that we understand that He does not create us nor nurture us merely to be like beasts in the universe; rather He creates us and nurtures us for a purpose and for a method of obligation that we follow. This is so that He may make us become familiar with the word Allah before the word Lord. In this there is an indication that the purpose of obligation is the welfare of society and your welfare among yourselves, for the Creator, glorified is He, did not create us in vain, nor leave us neglected, a created thing without any purpose.

Therefore at the beginning of Surat al-Rahman the Truth, glorified is He, makes clear that teaching the method precedes the formation of creation, and that creation is not counted as a blessing except when it is accomplished within the framework of the Creator's method, for the owner of a craft must determine its function before he makes it. He said: ﴿The Most Merciful, taught the Qur'an, created man, taught him expression﴾ [al-Rahman: 1-4].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿to Him belongs sovereignty (al-mulk)﴾. The root (m-l-k) yields al-mulk, al-milk and al-malakut. Al-milk (with a kasra) is what you possess, even if it is little; al-mulk (with a damma) is that you have authority over whoever possesses; and al-milk and al-mulk belong to the visible world, whereas al-malakut is what we do not see of Allah's sovereignty, which Allah does not reveal except to whom He chooses among His prophets, messengers, and the people of His obedience, whose natural disposition (fitrah) of faith is purified and whose receiving apparatus from Allah is sound. These Allah makes to see some of His malakut. Therefore, when our master Ibrahim fulfilled and submitted to his Lord's command, He showed him this malakut: ﴿And thus We showed Ibrahim the malakut of the heavens and the earth...﴾ [al-An'am: 75].

Like mulk and malakut, we say rahmah and rahamut, and rahbah and rahbut.

The meaning of "to Him belongs sovereignty" is: if you have witnessed a vast dominion, know that it belongs to the One who created you. And it is remarkable that it was created for your sake, and Allah created it for you before He created you; for the first man came into a cosmos prepared to receive him, with all that he needs of the means of life, beginning with the earth, the sky, the sun, the moon and the stars, down to the smallest thing in the universe.

His following saying: ﴿There is no god but He﴾ means: this wondrous creation belongs to Allah alone, and no one has claimed it for himself. And since no one has claimed creation for himself, no one may claim that he is the author of the method by which man lives in the universe; for the One who created is the One who lays down the method, and the One who made is the One who lays down the law of maintenance for His making.

﴿Then how are you turned away?﴾ means: how do you turn away from worshipping Allah the Creator to worshipping others who have no share of creation whatsoever? How do you turn away from a Lord who created and nurtured and still does, who has not abandoned us, and who has not handed over His creation to anyone else, nor is He prepared ever to hand it over.

Having first moved the creatures with mention of lordship (rubūbiyyah), by which He created, nurtured and commanded, and with mention of divinity (ulūhiyyah), which guarantees the wellbeing of lands and their people, the Glorified One then made clear that He is free of need of His creation. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is not in need of you﴾, meaning: He is independent of your faith, and your acts of obedience do not benefit Him.

He, glorified is He, made the obligations (taklīf) for the sake of the soundness of your own condition, not for a benefit that returns to Him, glorified is He. You are His creation and His handiwork, and the craftsman wants to see his handiwork in the best state. He wants to see the believing servant in a believing society whose movement supports one another and does not collide, and whose orientations agree and do not clash. The Creator, glorified is He, does not like to see His creatures fighting one another, one building while the other destroys.

So this is the purpose of creation and of the method (manhaj), because Allah, exalted is He, created the creation through His attributes of perfection, and the creation did not add to Him a single attribute He did not have before. Therefore He has no need of you. You are only His handiwork, and He wants good for you...

As for the meaning of His words, ﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is not in need of you﴾, and His words, glorified is He: ﴿and He does not approve disbelief for His servants﴾, this is evidence of His love for His creation. It is as if He, exalted is He, says: I am independent of you, but I do not like you to be disbelievers, because I want to make you a source of pride before My angels, who said of you: ﴿Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood, while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]...

So the Truth, glorified is He, does not approve disbelief for His servants because they are His creation and His handiwork. He, glorified is He, is keen on what sets them right, keen that they be believers so that their affairs may be made straight, and His blessings extend to them from this world to the Hereafter. Just as He bestowed upon them blessings for a limited time in this world, He wants to bestow upon them blessings in the Hereafter, and the blessings of the Hereafter are lasting and eternal...

﴿And if you are grateful, He approves it for you﴾: if you are grateful, He approves gratitude for you, is pleased with it from you, loves it for you, and rewards you with good for it. He, glorified is He, approved gratitude for them only because it is the cause of their happiness in this world and the Hereafter, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾ [Ibrahim: 7]. Gratitude for a blessing brings us more blessing; we are grateful for it, and it gives us more, and so gratitude remains continual and the blessing remains continual...

﴿Then to your Lord is your return﴾: meaning, if I have begun your creation with honour for you, and you have met this honour with ingratitude and have not rendered its due by believing in Me and obeying My method, then know that you will return to Me and will not escape from Me, ﴿then He will inform you of what you used to do﴾, that is, He will tell you what you did.

﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ [az-Zumar: 7]. So remember this matter always, and take its reckoning into account before it is too late.

This verse is a warning from the Truth, glorified is He, and an explanation of the punishment, which by its nature deters people from crimes, so that the punishment does not occur at all. This is from the mercy of the Creator toward creation: He, glorified is He, wants good for them, and wants them to enjoy His blessings in the Hereafter as they enjoyed His blessings in this world.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 39, verse 8:

The (ḍurr) is that which takes a person out of his soundness in himself, or in those he supports, or in what he owns. When harm befalls a person, it deprives him of the pillar of arrogance, because he does not hand himself over without a price, and he knows that no one removes his harm except Allah, so he turns to Him alone and does not deceive himself...

Likewise, when harm touches a person and his means become difficult for him, he does not resort except to his Lord, after the ground of "Nay, indeed, man transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient" (al-'Alaq: 6-7) has collapsed in him, and after the mask of haughtiness and arrogance has fallen from him...

So when harm befalls a person, while he knows that harm is lifted only by Allah and turned away only by the Creator of the heavens and the earth, he turns to no one but Him. Whoever his inner perceptions (mawajid) believe is able to lift this harm, even if he is a disbeliever in Allah, not believing in Him, when harm touches him he says: "O Lord." What is remarkable is that Allah accepts him, relieves him, and does not turn him away: "Or who answers the distressed one when he calls upon Him and removes the evil?" (al-Naml: 62).

It suffices you that you find no one but Me, and you say nothing but "O Lord." Therefore He, glory be to Him, said: "And when harm touches you at sea, those whom you call upon vanish except Him" (al-Isra': 67), meaning: if you call upon other than Allah, it cannot reach you, it loses the way to you, and none answers you but Allah.

The meaning of munīban ilayhi (turning penitently to Him) is returning to Him. "Then when He grants him a blessing from Himself" (al-Zumar: 8), meaning: He gives him, "he forgets what he used to call upon Him for before" (al-Zumar: 8). The scholars raised an uproar and a debate concerning the relative pronoun (mā) here, and they said: why did it not say "nasiya man" (he forgot whoever), since man indicates the rational, whereas (mā) is for the non-rational, on the basis that (mā) here refers to Allah, may He be exalted.

We say: the Qur'an does not proceed in this manner. Read: "Say: O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship, nor are you worshippers of what I worship" (al-Kafirun: 1-3). Here (mā) is applied to Allah, may He be exalted. Thus (mā) here is in its correct meaning, even if the wisdom of that escapes you. Yes, man is for the rational and mā for the non-rational, but the Truth, glory be to Him, did not describe Himself with reason, because reason is your attribute, so He came with an attribute that does not preclude the absence of reason. Had He said man, He would have included the Truth, glory be to Him, among those who reason, whereas He did not describe Himself as rational; rather He is "the Knower and the All-Knowing" (ʿAlīm wa-ʿAllām).

This difficulty can be avoided if we give (mā) a different interpretation, so the meaning becomes: he forgets the harm that was the cause of his return to Allah, not that he forgets Him who rescued him and removed his harm; and mā then retains its linguistic meaning for the non-rational.

And His saying: "And he sets up rivals to Allah, to lead astray from His way." Andād is the plural of nidd, which is the like, the equal, or the counterpart. These disbelievers ascribed rivals to Allah, the Exalted, even though they knew He is the true God, glory be to Him, and even though they knew that "those whom you call upon vanish except Him," in order to satisfy within themselves the perceptions of the faith-inclined nature (al-fitra al-imaniyya). Each one of them wants to have a god to worship, but a god according to his own desire, a god who has no obligations, whose worship imposes no hardship on the self, a god without a method: no "do," and no "do not."

As for His saying "to lead astray from His way," some read it with a fatha (liyaḍilla, "that he may go astray"). We say: he did not do that except because he himself is astray, so the closer reading is with a ḍamma (liyuḍilla, "to lead [others] astray"), meaning: he leads others astray.

Then He, glory be to Him, says "Say" (qul), meaning: reply, O Muhammad. "Say: Enjoy your disbelief a little; indeed you are among the companions of the Fire" (al-Zumar: 8). But what is the manner of enjoying disbelief? We say: that one worships a god without a method and without obligations, a god who does not prevent him from drinking wine and does not restrain the desires of his soul, a god who does not command him to truthfulness or trustworthiness... etc. Rather, He leaves him to roam the universe, enjoying it as he wishes.

He said "a little" because the enjoyment here is limited to the world and the duration of his remaining in it. We have said that the world, for a human being, is the period of his remaining in it, not its duration from the creation of Adam until the Hour.

And the phrase "among the companions of the Fire": the word companionship (ṣuḥba) here indicates familiarity and intimate affection between the Fire and its people. Therefore, in addressing the Fire, He, exalted, says: "On the Day We say to Hell, 'Are you filled?' and it says, 'Is there more?'" (Qaf: 30), meaning: bring my beloved and my companions, and to Me with more of them.

Then Almighty God says: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, wary of the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord...﴾

The particle (*am*) indicates a choice between two things: one says "this or that." So it must have a counterpart. The counterpart of ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night...﴾ [az-Zumar: 9] is in the verse before it, where God says: ﴿When harm touches man, he calls upon his Lord, turning to Him in repentance. Then when He bestows upon him a favour from Himself, he forgets what he had been calling upon Him for before, and sets up rivals to God in order to lead [others] astray from His way...﴾ [az-Zumar: 8].

The meaning is: which of the two is better? The first, who when harm touches him humbly calls upon God, but when the harm is removed sets up rivals to God; or the one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, wary of the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord.

The word *qanit* (devoutly obedient, from *qunut*, constant submission and worship) means one who is constantly humble and devoted in worship.

His words "wary of the Hereafter" mean he fears it and the subjugation (*qahr*) within it. And "hoping for the mercy of his Lord" is because His mercy precedes His wrath. He did not say "secure" as the counterpart of "wary." Rather, He first mentioned what frightens one about the Hereafter if one disobeys. What is meant is that he fears the Fire in the Hereafter. But when He spoke of God's mercy, He placed it directly, saying ﴿and hoping for the mercy of his Lord﴾, and did not say "and hoping for Paradise."

The believer, when he hopes, does not hope in his deeds and his striving in this world. Rather, he hopes and awaits the mercy of God, because he is not saved by his deeds. For any person, however righteous, when he is subjected to a precise reckoning, must come out with sins and condemnation.

So, the guarantee for all of us, the thing that encompasses us, is God's mercy, as came in the noble hadith: "No one will enter Paradise by his deeds." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Not even I, unless God envelops me with His mercy."

So beware of being deceived by your deeds, for all the obligations are for your own benefit, and nothing of them returns to God. So when He rewards you for them in the Hereafter, that is a bounty and a blessing from God.

Then He, glorified is He, says: ﴿Say: "Are those who know equal to those who do not know?"﴾ After Almighty God had drawn a comparison between the man who, when harm touches him, calls upon his Lord turning to Him in repentance, then when He bestows a favour upon him he forgets what he had been calling upon Him for before, and the one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, wary of the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord.

He, glorified is He, wished to affirm this meaning and to show us that the people of true knowledge are not equal to the people of non-true knowledge. ﴿Say: "Are those who know equal to those who do not know?"﴾ So the one who returned to disbelief after God had removed his harm did not possess true knowledge, for if he had known it he would not have returned to disbelief, and he would have considered what is demanded of him in this world insignificant when compared with what has been prepared for him as reward in the Hereafter.

As for the one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, wary of the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord, he has attained true knowledge. Devotion (*qunut*) at night has many aspects. First: it is further from ostentation (*riya'*) and seeking to be heard (*sum'ah*). Second: all his limbs are free to meet his Lord. The eye, for example, in the darkness of the night, rests from the sights that occupy a person and take his attention, because every sight takes a part of your thoughts: this one leaves, that one comes, this one speaks, and that one...

But the night is stillness with no preoccupation in it. So all the limbs are sincerely for the sake of God's countenance; sights and sounds do not occupy them. This atmosphere provides you with a true and humble standing before God.

In devotion you abandon sleep and deprive yourself of its comfort, to stand before your Lord, prostrating or standing. This is the attribute of the people of devotion who spend the night in intimate conversation with their Lord. This is also the state of the one who travels through the Book of God, who does not reach the *sin* of "an-Nas" [the last surah] until he begins again with "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" at its beginning. Therefore we have said before: the whole Qur'an is built on continuity (*wasl*), not on pausing (*waqf*).

So can one whose state is this be equal to one who disbelieves in God? This is knowledge and action together. As for one who does not act upon what he knows, or who knows but does not put his knowledge to use for his benefit... Then, when a servant knows and acts upon his knowledge, God pours abundance upon him...

Therefore God, glorified is He, said in the sacred hadith: "My servant does not draw near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him. And My servant continues to draw near to Me with voluntary acts until I love him. When I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he strikes, and his foot with which he walks. And if he asks Me, I will surely give to him..."

And His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿Only people of understanding remember.﴾

That is: the people of thinking minds who investigate sensible things and reflect upon the signs. For a human being has senses that perceive and an intellect that weighs and chooses. So he takes this by hearing, that by sight, and this by smell, then presents them to the intellect to consider what good and what evil is in them. If the intellect is sound, it prefers the good and chooses from among the alternatives the most beneficial and most useful.

Piety (taqwa) means guarding yourself against acts of disobedience, and placing between yourself and the attributes of majesty of God a shield. God is the Compelling, the Subduer, the Possessor of retribution, so place between yourself and these attributes a shield that protects you.

His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, fear your Lord﴾ — that is, in the obligations — ﴿For those who do good in this world is good﴾ — that is, good in the Hereafter. He did not say "for those who do good, a good [reward] in this world," because the disbelievers enjoy in this world many good things of wealth, status, and knowledge, etc.

If we interpret "good" (ḥasanah) as bounty (ni'mah), then bounty that becomes a cause for turning a person away from his Lord is not counted as good but as evil. Therefore, the good intended here is in the Hereafter. ﴿And God's earth is spacious﴾ — but what is the connection between ﴿And God's earth is spacious﴾ and His saying ﴿fear your Lord﴾?

They said: it means that if you encounter hardships in the land where you live, then God's earth is spacious, so seek protection for yourself and your religion in another land, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And whoever emigrates in the way of God will find on the earth many a refuge and abundance﴾ [al-Nisa': 100].

And He said with the same meaning: ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves — [the angels] will say, "In what [condition] were you?" They will say, "We were oppressed in the land." [The angels] will say, "Was not the earth of God spacious that you could emigrate therein?"﴾ [al-Nisa': 97].

So: when your land becomes narrow for you, and when the noose tightens around you in it, seek another land where you can be safe for yourself and your religion, and for applying the method of God without opposition and without obstruction.

And if we were attentive to a verse in Surat al-Rahman, we would find in it a solution to all the problems of the contemporary world, namely His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the earth He has set for the creatures﴾ [al-Rahman: 10].

That is: He made the earth — all the earth, without specification — under the disposal of all creatures, also without specification. Every human being has a share in God's earth, so if a place becomes too narrow for him, he has a right to another place. But human laws and interests have altered this picture, and placed obstacles, hindrances, and complicated procedures in the way of this freedom which the Creator, glorified is He, guaranteed for movement on His earth.

Therefore we find that the economic problem of the world lies in the existence of land without men, or men without land. If we left the earth to God as He created it for His servants, if we made the earth all the earth for the creatures all the creatures, we would have resolved all the problems of the world...

Then He, glorified is He, says: ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account﴾ [al-Zumar: 10]. The exhortation to patience after His saying ﴿And God's earth is spacious﴾ [al-Zumar: 10] indicates that there must exist in life difficulties, problems, and hardships that require patience...

So the Truth, glorified is He, wants us to bear the method of God, to act by it so as to make ourselves happy, then to rise in faith, and to try to make others happy so that goodness spreads throughout society. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "May God make radiant the face of a man who heard my statement, memorized it, and then conveyed it to one who had not heard it, for many a one who conveys understands better than one who hears."

So: transmitting good to others is good for you too, and its benefit will return to you, because when you withhold knowledge of good from others, those others will be in evil, and this evil will trouble you and some of it will reach you. So it is in your own interest that good should pervade others, and in your interest that others be good, neither stealing, nor cursing, nor betraying, nor transgressing against others. Thus transmitting the knowledge of good to others is beneficial to the one who transmits it, at least in restraining the evil of the evil-doer from him.

The patient person is one who endures hardships and trials that remove him from: soundness of the limbs, soundness of wealth, and soundness of family. The patient person is certain that his pain and harm will give him better than the bounty he lost before the pain and harm, because God said: ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account.﴾

If obligations have an accounting with God — prayer has an accounting, zakat has an accounting, etc. — then the reward of patience is without accounting, meaning: unknown...

And patience is not doubting the mercy of God, and not objecting to His judgment and decree...

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 39, verse 11:

Qur'anic text: ﴿Say: Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion. And I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit.﴾

We note in this verse the repetition of the verb "umirtu" (I have been commanded), and this indicates that we are before two commands, each independent of the other. The first command, ﴿Say: Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion﴾ [al-Zumar: 11-12], is a command for the certainty of faith and the certainty of worship, such that we direct it purely to Allah.

Sincerity to Allah (ikhlas) comes in stages. One worships Allah in expectation of His reward and in longing for His Paradise; another worships Him out of fear of His Fire; and another worships Him for His own sake, because He deserves to be worshipped and to be loved for His own sake.

Therefore, He, glorified is He, said at the end of Surat al-Kahf: ﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 110]. Not the Paradise of his Lord, nor the reward of his Lord. Rather, he desires the meeting and desires intimacy with Allah, so the blessing does not preoccupy him; rather, what preoccupies him is the companionship of the Bestower, glorified is He. ﴿Let him do righteous deeds and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 110]. And Paradise is one (of the things that could be sought).

So: the first command is specific to beliefs (aqa'id). As for the other command, ﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit﴾ [al-Zumar: 12], it concerns the Islamic obligations of "do" and "do not." But how does the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say...

...How can the Messenger of God say, "I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims" (surah 39:12)? Is he not already the first of them in fact? The first obligation placed on him was at the moment the revelation came down to him, before he conveyed it to his companions. So there was a period during which he, may God bless him and grant him peace, was the first to submit to God, the first to submit his way to God, before he conveyed this way. This is if we take the word in its primary sense.

Also, he has a priority in implementing the rulings before people, after he conveys the way to them, so that they know that the message was not meant to pamper the messengers, but to establish an example among them. When the messengers themselves act upon God's way, they teach all people that this way is good, as evidenced by the fact that they bound themselves to it in practice before they bound the people to it, as in the saying: "I have not commanded you to do anything without first doing it myself."

Another matter: God Most High deprived the Messenger, and the People of his House, of what He gave to the common Muslims. The deceased is inherited by his family, but no one inherits from the Messenger of God among his family, and the poor among the Muslims in general may take from the funds of zakat and charity, whereas the Family of the House are forbidden to take from them.

So the Messenger of God bore hardships in the cause of the message, and it was not for him a luxury or a pampering; likewise, his household bore it with him, and part of these hardships befell them. Were it not that the brightness of the reward in their souls gave them hope and confidence in Paradise, a confidence that made them, as it were, looking at the people of Paradise in Paradise enjoying bliss and at the people of the Fire in the Fire being tormented, they would not have endured these trials and hardships.

Therefore, when He addresses the wives of the Prophet, He says: "O wives of the Prophet, you are not like any other of women" (surah 33:32). Because you are the wives of the Prophet, you must be the first to implement the Messenger's way, so that through you the example is realized, and so that people know that the Messenger did not come as a tyrant commanding them to what he himself does not do, or forbidding them from what he himself does not refrain from; rather, in implementation he is ahead of them, their leader and their exemplar, he and his household. Thus, he, may God bless him and grant him peace, was the first of the Muslims in fact.

There is a long discussion among the scholars on the question of "the first of the Muslims," since it also occurred on the tongue of Moses, peace be upon him, who said: "and I am the first of the believers" (surah 6:163), meaning the Muslims of his time. As for the Messenger of God, he is the first of the Muslims in his own time and in the time of others. To bring this matter closer, we say: the priority here is a priority of excellence, and excellence may be relative, as when we say: "So-and-so is first in the Faculty of Law this year," where the excellence is specific to the year we are speaking of, and perhaps in other years someone surpassed him and obtained higher grades than him; and excellence may be general, as if we said: "So-and-so is first in the Faculty of Law since it was founded."

Thus, priority may be in time, and priority may be in comparing eras with one another. If a messenger from among the messengers says, "I am the first of the Muslims," the meaning is the first of the Muslims in his time. But if it is said to Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, "I am the first of the Muslims," the meaning is the first of the Muslims from Adam until the Hour is established. That is to say: although my time is later, I am first when we take the rank at the moment of the obligation. Furthermore, other messengers were sent to a specific time in a specific place, whereas I was sent to all people in every time and place. Furthermore, I am the Seal of the Messengers, so there is no messenger after me, and no one follows up on the messengers after my message. These are all the grounds of priority for the Messenger of God, and they are apparent grounds that cannot be denied.

Therefore we find priority always on the tongue of the Messenger of God, as in the saying of the Most High: "Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, then I am the first of the worshippers" (surah 43:81), meaning: the first to affirm this matter.

Glory be to God! Would the Messenger of God say, "Indeed I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous day"? It is as if he is saying: I have not attained this rank as an absolute ruling that I am a noble prophet; rather, I am like the common people: if I disobey my Lord, I expose myself to punishment. That is, God's preference for me first and His choosing me does not intercede for me if disobedience occurs from me.

Subhan Allah! Would the Messenger of Allah say: ﴿Indeed I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous day﴾ [Az-Zumar: 13]? It is as if he is saying: I have not attained this rank as an absolute judge that I am a noble prophet; rather I am like the common people: if I disobey my Lord, I expose myself to punishment. That is, Allah's preference for me first and His choosing of me will not intercede for me if an act of disobedience occurs from me.

Then Allah, Glorified is He, says on the tongue of His Messenger: ﴿Say: It is Allah I worship, sincere in my religion to Him﴾ [Az-Zumar: 14]. This too is for the beliefs and for the certainty of faith. His earlier saying has already preceded: ﴿Say: Indeed I have been commanded to worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [Az-Zumar: 11], and here ﴿Say: It is Allah I worship﴾ [Az-Zumar: 14]. So what is the difference between (Allahu a'bud, "Allah I worship") and (a'budu Allah, "I worship Allah")?

Allah's saying ﴿an a'buda Allah﴾ [Az-Zumar: 11] came in the natural order of the sentence: the verb, then the subject, then the object. A sentence in this order does not prevent coordinating with the object, just as you say: "Obey so-and-so," and it does not prevent us from saying "and so-and-so." But if we place the object before the verb, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿It is Allah I worship﴾ [Az-Zumar: 14], then the fronting of the object conveys restriction (qasr), that is: restricting worship to Allah alone, as if you say: "To Allah I complain," meaning: not to other than Him.

So the first verse came in the natural order of the sentence, while the other came in the form of restriction, as if he said: I do not worship other than Allah, and you, worship whatever you wish ﴿besides Him﴾ [Az-Zumar: 15].

Then Allah, Glorified is He, explains the consequence of associating partners with Him, saying:

﴿Say: Indeed the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, that is the manifest loss﴾ [Az-Zumar: 15].

We understand that these polytheists lost themselves on the Day of Resurrection, because they wronged themselves by disbelief and by association. But how do they also lose their families? It is said: their families are their children and offspring. These either believe, or they remain upon their disbelief together with the fathers. If they remain upon their disbelief, they are losers like their fathers. And if they believe, they will not be with the fathers, and they will be deprived of seeing them, because these are in Paradise and those are in the Fire. So loss clings to them in both cases.

The word "loss" here was emphasized by Allah, Glorified is He, with the absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq): ﴿That is indeed the manifest loss﴾ [Az-Zumar: 15]. Then He described the loss as "manifest" (mubin), that is: clear, evident, and encompassing. Because when does a merchant become a loser? Either his capital returns to him without increase, in which case he has lost his effort and labor in his trade; or the loss extends to the capital itself, so he loses his effort and labor and also part of his capital. This is the manifest loss, that is, the loss encompassing everything. So His saying, ﴿Unquestionably, that is the manifest loss﴾ [Az-Zumar: 15], means the all-encompassing loss that surrounds his family, his wealth, his labor, and his striving.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 39, verse 15:

... ﴿Say: Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, that is the manifest loss.﴾ We understand that these polytheists have lost themselves on the Day of Resurrection, because they wronged themselves by disbelief and by associating partners with God. But how do they also lose their families? They said: Because their families are their children and their offspring. These [children] will either believe, or they will remain upon their disbelief together with their fathers. If they remain upon their disbelief, they are losers just like their fathers. And if they believe, they will not be together with the fathers, and they will be deprived of seeing them, because those [believers] are in Paradise and those [disbelievers] are in the Fire. Thus, the loss is attached to them in both situations.

The word "loss" here has been emphasized by God, glory be to Him, with the absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq) ﴿That is the manifest loss﴾. Then He described the loss as "manifest" (mubin), that is: clear, evident and all-encompassing. For when is a merchant considered a loser? Either his capital is returned to him without increase, and in this case he has lost his effort and toil in his trade; or the loss extends to the capital itself, so that he loses his effort and toil and also part of his capital. This is the manifest loss, that is, the loss that encompasses everything. So His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Unquestionably, that is the manifest loss﴾ means the all-encompassing loss that surrounded its people, their wealth, their toil and their striving.

Almighty God explains the end of the disbelievers, saying: ﴿For them there will be layers of fire above them, and beneath them layers﴾ [az-Zumar: 16]. The word ẓulal (layers, canopies) is the plural of ẓullah, which is that which shades a person and protects him from the heat of the sun. In shade a person seeks rest and the coolness of the air. But as for these, they have layers of fire, not a single layer, and fire is never a shade at all.

So this is a style of mockery toward the disbelievers. Would that these layers were only from one direction; rather, they are from above them and from beneath them. A person, when harm comes to him from one direction, usually turns away to the opposite direction. In another place God, glory be to Him, says: ﴿For them there will be a bed of Hell, and above them coverings﴾ [al-A'raf: 41].

So the fire surrounds them, with no escape from it and no way of flight.

﴿That is what God frightens His servants with. O My servants, so fear Me﴾. Reflect on the mercy of God toward His servants, even in the context of mentioning the Fire and the punishment. The Fire is not meant to torment creation; rather, it is meant to frighten them and deter them so that they do not stand in this position and do not expose themselves to this punishment. You do not do this except with someone you love, just as you frighten your son about failing, and explain to him the consequence of negligence and what humiliation, abasement and contempt he will face if he fails in his studies.

So His purpose, exalted is He, in mentioning the Fire is that He frightens with it, so that creation does not fall into the causes that lead to it. The intelligent person, when he is frightened, fears, and when he is restrained, he is restrained and withholds himself. This frightening is considered one of the greatest blessings of God upon him...

Therefore He said after it: ﴿O My servants, so fear Me﴾, meaning: make My frightening of you a mercy to you, not a terrorizing of you. When a person weighs matters and compares the state of the people of Paradise with the state of the people of the Fire, he must take heed and return to the right path, and then he becomes worthy of God's mercy and forgiveness. So, among the blessings of God upon us is that He frightens us, warns us of evil before it occurs, and does not seize us unawares or leave us in heedlessness.

The word ṭāghūt is an intensive form of ṭāghin (one who transgresses), and ṭāghūt is the tyrant who grows in arrogance when people respect his oppression or fear him, which increases his wrongdoing and insolence. The ṭāghūt must have some kind of directive authority and exaltation, which is why idols are not called ṭawāghīt, for they do not exalt themselves by their own essence and have no directives; rather, it is their worshippers who elevate them. Therefore, ṭāghūt applies only to human beings, even if they are only rulers. Otherwise, what is the aspect of tyranny in idols? Idols neither speak nor oppress...

[And] a person becomes a ṭāghūt only because people feared him and did not repel his tyranny or confront him, but rather agreed with him and flattered him, so his tyranny spread.

Some hold that ṭāghūt is everything worshipped besides God, but we should add to that: and it is content with this worship.
