On the basis of this definition, idols are not counted as ṭawāghīt, nor is ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) counted as a ṭāghūt, nor are the friends of God (awliyāʾ Allāh) counted as ṭawāghīt as some claim, because people were tested through them, and they bear no blame for that.

As for His saying: ﴿And they turned back to God﴾, meaning: they returned to worshipping Him alone, without partner, ﴿for them is good news﴾, meaning: of Paradise, because they stood against tyranny, rejected oppression and did not accept it. God, exalted is He, wants the Muslim society to stand against every tyrant, to correct the conduct of every deviant, and to boycott the people of corruption and isolate them from society and from the movement of life within it.

We illustrate this with the thug who carries a weapon and threatens people in their lives, their livelihoods and their honor; indeed, some of them defy the law, the authority and the system. He has only reached this level because society abandoned its role in reform and in confronting the people of evil...

From His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they turned back to God﴾, meaning: they returned to Him, we understand that they were with God first and then deviated from Him. How? They say: because every person was with God upon the first natural disposition of faith when God took the covenant from all creation, saying: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ They said: ﴿Yes, we testify﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 172]. But among them are those who remained upon this covenant and this sound disposition, and among them are those who deviated from it and forgot it.

Therefore the Qur'an often says "remembrance" (dhikr), meaning: of the first covenant. So the meaning of ﴿they turned back to God﴾ is: they returned to the innate faith and to the first covenant, or they returned to God for recompense on the Day of Resurrection.

As for His words, glorified is He: ﴿For them is good news﴾, al-bushrā is the pleasing news which we announce before its time. Good news is of two kinds: the removal of harm and pain, or the realization of a wish and hope. Those who avoided ṭāghūt, not worshipping it, and turned back to God, both of these were realized for them together: first, they were freed from the Fire and its pains; then their wish was fulfilled by entering Paradise, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has certainly triumphed﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 185].

Therefore He said after it: ﴿So give good news to My servants﴾ [al-Zumar: 17], meaning with this pleasing good news...

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah 39, verse 18

Those who listen to speech and follow the best of it. Speech must come from a speaker. When people listen to speech from a speaker, they follow the best of what is said, and what is said comes from the best of speakers. When we look at the best of speakers, we find none but Allah, glorified and exalted. So when Allah commands a ruling and you follow it, His word is the best speech and His command is the most beneficial command.

Allah, glorified is He, does not benefit from His commands to you, and your disobedience does not harm Him. You are therefore the ones who benefit from the methodology (manhaj), the ones who gain from implementing it. Then you are the creation of Allah and His handiwork, and it is grievous to Him, glorified is He, that this handiwork should go astray or be punished.

Then He, glorified is He, desires through His methodology and His law that He should continue His giving and His blessings upon you, and that the blessings of this world be connected for you with the blessings of the Hereafter...

Or: "the best of what is said" means Islam. Islam came when people were of diverse kinds: disbelievers who do not believe in a god, polytheists who believe in a god alongside other gods, and adherents of religions that had earlier scriptures and messengers, such as the Jews and the Christians. Those who lived contemporaneously with Islam, if they listen, will listen to this speech and that speech; they listen to the disbelievers, the atheists, the polytheists, and the people of the earlier scriptures.

It is as if Allah, glorified is He, is saying: present these sayings to your minds, choose the best of them, and do not be fanatical toward a saying without examining it and comparing it with others. If you do this, and if this objectivity is available to you, you will find nothing but Islam to be the best of sayings and the most worthy of being followed. It is the religion that gathered for people every good and kept them far from every evil.

It is the religion that came as a guardian (muhaymin) over all the religions before it, and its Book is the guardian over all the books before it. Islam came as a religion general in time and in place. Therefore it is the seal of religions, after which there is no religion, and no book after its Book, and no messenger after its Messenger.

A religion with these attributes must have perfected all the conditions of perfection, as He, glorified is He, said: "This day I have perfected for you your religion, completed My favour upon you, and approved for you Islam as a religion" [al-Ma'idah: 3]. Islam, therefore, is the best of religions, the best of sayings, and the best that we follow.

Then the verses continue describing the believers who avoided the taghut (false deities), so that they did not worship them, and who turned in repentance to Allah, and who listen to speech and follow the best of it: "Those are the ones whom Allah has guided, and those are the people of understanding" [al-Zumar: 18]. "Guided" (hadahum) means He indicated to them and directed them. When they followed His indication and guidance, and there was no obstinacy in their souls against this indication, He gave them the guidance of success (tawfiq) and faith, so they believed...

Likewise, Allah, glorified is He, gives His servant the guidance of indication and direction (hidayat al-dalalah wa al-irshad), and this is for the believer and the disbeliever alike. Whoever obeys in the first receives the second, which is the guidance of help (hidayat al-ma'unah), and this is for the believer and not the disbeliever. It is as if Allah, exalted is He, says to His believing servant: "You have believed in Me, heard My word, and obeyed, so I will help you to obey and make its matter easy for you, and I will make the matter of disobedience difficult for you."

This is among the greatest blessings of Allah upon the servant: that He facilitates for him the matter of obedience, helps him bear its hardships, and in return closes off from him the doors of disobedience and its incentives. This is the meaning of His saying: "And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and gives them their God-consciousness" [Muhammad: 17].

So the meaning of "He increased them in guidance" is: He gave them the guidance of help in faith.

As for His saying: "And those are the people of understanding" (ulu al-albab), it means: the possessors of thinking, considered minds, because they laid out before themselves all the sayings, examined them, compared between them, and took the best of them, which achieves for them happiness, benefit, and harmony in the movement of life without conflict, but rather a straight, mutually supportive movement that removes from hearts resentment, rancour and envy, and prevents deviation such as theft, deceit, bribery, usurpation, and so on.

Who would oppose such a methodology? Who would reject it? It is a straight methodology, to which the sound intellect has no choice but to submit and to walk in its guidance. Therefore Allah named those who chose this methodology "ulu al-albab" [al-Zumar: 18], that is, the people of intellect. The task of the intellect is to reason about thought so that it does not wander, but rather to present matters and choose from among the alternatives what sets it right. But the bane of opinion is desire, for desire is what turns you away from the dictates of reason to the dictates of desire.

Another view says: the intended meaning of His saying "those who listen to speech and follow the best of it" is that it refers specifically to those who listen to the sayings of Islam and follow the best of these sayings. Therefore the comparative form "best" (ahsan) was used, as if in Islam there is "a good saying" and "a better saying." This view does not take the matter in its generality, but makes it specific to the sayings of Islam, all of which are characterized by goodness, but among them there is good and better, and people of contemplative minds choose the best among them.

An example of this: Islam prescribed, for instance, retaliation (qisas) against the killer, prescribed blood money (diyah) upon him, and also prescribed pardon. He, glorified is He, said: "But whoever is pardoned by his brother in any way, then grant him reasonable compensation and pay him with kindness..." [al-Baqarah: 178]. So whoever takes retaliation or blood money takes the good, and whoever rises to pardon takes the best.

Likewise, in His saying: "If you disclose your charities, they are excellent; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you..." [al-Baqarah: 271]. If you display charity, you are not sinful; rather, it is a good matter, but the better of it is that you conceal it.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 39, verse 19:

The Prophet (ﷺ) loved his community, was eager to guide them and to take them by the hand, and it pained him that any one of them should deviate from his method or oppose him. The noble Qur'an addresses this matter in more than one place. In Surah ash-Shu'ara': ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 3].

In al-Kahf: ﴿So perhaps you would destroy yourself with grief over their traces, if they do not believe in this message, in sorrow﴾ [al-Kahf: 6].

And He said: ﴿So let not your soul go out in pursuit of them through regrets...﴾ [Fatir: 8].

So the Truthful One (Al-Haqq), glory be to Him, consoles His Messenger, saying to him: O Muhammad, do not grieve over these people, for they have deserved the punishment, and God's judgment upon them is that they will be punished. ﴿Is then someone upon whom the word of punishment has come due...﴾ [az-Zumar: 19]. "Haqqa" means: it was established from God, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The word has come into effect from Me: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind all together"﴾ [as-Sajdah: 13].

Since the punishment has come due upon them, why would you grieve? ﴿Would you then save those who are in the Fire?﴾ [az-Zumar: 19]. The becoming-due of the word of punishment here is not a compulsion upon the servant to act; rather, it is a knowledge that he will do such-and-such, so God knew what would come from them and recorded it against them. Thus the becoming-due here is not a universal becoming-due willed by the Creator, glory be to Him; rather, it is because He, glory be to Him, knew in advance what they would choose.

We have previously addressed this matter in discussing His saying, exalted is He: ﴿May the hands of Abu Lahab perish, and perish he! * His wealth will not avail him, nor what he gained. * He will burn in a Fire of blazing flame﴾ [al-Masad: 1-3]. This is a judgment from God upon Abu Lahab that he will burn in a Fire of blazing flame. This judgment came and was conveyed by the Messenger of God, and Abu Lahab heard it while he was alive and provided for. Did Muhammad (ﷺ) feel secure that Abu Lahab would stand in a gathering of people and say: "I bear witness that there is no god but God, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God," saying it even if hypocritically, and appear before people as a believer? In that case, would he be contradicting the word of God?

Abu Lahab was a disbeliever, just as Khalid, 'Amr and 'Ikrimah were disbelievers, and it was within his power to believe as they believed. But God knew that he would not believe, even after this destiny was conveyed to him in an inimitable Qur'an that is preserved by those who recite it and recited until the Day of Resurrection. Thus this verse indicates that God, exalted is He, knew in advance that he would not believe, and He did not compel him not to believe.

So the Truthful One says to His Messenger: Do not let your soul go out in pursuit of them through regrets, for God has judged them, because of His knowledge of what would come from them, that they are among the people of the Fire. How, then, would you save them, when God has judged them to be so?

We note in the style of the verse ﴿Is then someone upon whom the word of punishment has come due...﴾ [az-Zumar: 19] that the verb "haqqa" was not marked with the feminine ending, although its subject "kalimah" (word) is feminine. They said: because the feminine here is not real (haqiqi), it is permissible for the verb to lack the feminine marker.

The interrogative in ﴿Is then someone upon whom the word of punishment has come due...﴾ [az-Zumar: 19] requires a predicate whose implied form is: "Is then the one upon whom the word of punishment has come due, do you wish to deliver him or protect him from it, by insisting that he believe? Do you wish to rescue him from the Fire, when God has judged that he is among its people?"

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 39, verse 20:

We have said that among the features of the Qur'anic style is that it mentions opposites, for the opposite reveals the goodness of its opposite, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in pleasure. And indeed, the wicked will be in Hellfire﴾ [al-Infitar: 13–14].

Here, after the Mighty and Majestic mentioned the disbelievers, against whom the word of punishment has come into effect, He mentions their counterpart, namely the God-conscious (al-muttaqun). ﴿But﴾ (lakin) is a qualification of what preceded: ﴿for those who feared their Lord are chambers, above which are built chambers, beneath which rivers flow…﴾ [al-Zumar: 20]. This contrast prepares the soul to deplore the worse counterpart and to beautify the higher one.

Ghuraf (chambers) is the plural of ghurfah, which is the private, detached space of a house, and it is derived from ghurfat al-ma' (a handful of water). ﴿For them are chambers, above which are chambers…﴾ [al-Zumar: 20]. Then He described the upper ones as ﴿built﴾ (mabniyyah) [al-Zumar: 20], because the custom with the lower chamber is that it is given care in its foundation, which carries the remaining stories. So He wished to draw our attention to the fact that the upper chambers too are built and cared for, no less distinguished than the lower chambers. Thus all the chambers, from the lowest to the highest, are distinguished.

Then reflect on the miracle in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾ [al-Zumar: 20]. Beneath which of them? Beneath both. If you say, "How?", we say: read His saying, may blessings and peace be upon him, in describing Paradise:

And in another place He, glorified is He, said: ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾ [al-Tawbah: 72]. There is a difference between tahtiha (beneath it) and min tahtiha (from beneath it). If we said "rivers flow beneath it", the meaning would be that the rivers come from another place and pass by it, so the upper one could block the water from the lower one.

As for ﴿from beneath which rivers flow﴾ [al-Zumar: 20], the spring of water flows from beneath these chambers, so its water is self-originating within them, having no supply from outside them. Therefore the waters in them are self-contained.

So you marvel because you measure matters by your own engineering, while your Lord, glorified is He, has a different engineering, coming in ways other than you imagine. For the thing that no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and that has not occurred to the heart, language has nothing to indicate it. Meanings exist first, then words are set down to signify them. If meanings do not exist, from where would the word come?

We now know, for example, (the television), and we know what it is. But before it was invented, did we know it or know its name? Therefore we have previously said: to the one who says God does not exist, may God protect us, we say: your speech is refuted by your own speech, for "God" is the subject and "does not exist" is the predicate. So from where did you come to know the word "God" if God does not exist? Therefore your saying "God does not exist" is proof that He exists, for the non-existent has no word. Whatever the ear does not hear, the eye does not see, and does not occur to the mind, has no name.

Therefore, when our Lord describes Paradise to us, He says: ﴿A description of Paradise which the God-conscious have been promised…﴾ [Muhammad: 15]. That is, He gives us a likeness of it, not the thing itself, because your language does not contain the words that express these meanings that are in Paradise. Nevertheless, at the moment He gives us the likeness, He negates from it what contradicts what exists in this world. So when He describes the wine of the Hereafter, He says: ﴿in which there is no intoxication, nor are they affected by it﴾ [al-Saffat: 47].

That is: it does not assault the intellect nor veil it as the wine of this world veils it. In a human being there is a gland responsible for balance; when he drinks wine, the wine overpowers this gland, depriving him of his balance and veiling his mind, so he sways here and there and raves with words whose meaning he does not know.

The wine of the Hereafter is not like this; the wine of the Hereafter gives you delight and joy without assaulting the intellect. ﴿Nor are they affected by it﴾ [al-Saffat: 47]. Nazf (draining) and nazh (drawing off) have the same meaning. You say: nazahat al-bi'r, meaning: I drew out what was in it of water. So nazf is the drawing out of what is in the belly. In a healthy, sound constitution, the body performs a process that we call elimination, such as the ear canal, sweat and urine, and this elimination is a sign of soundness and health of the body.

But there is elimination without soundness, like one who eats and then vomits what he has eaten, and may vomit blood from the inside of himself, may God protect us; or urine may come out continuously, as in one who suffers from incontinence, for example. Among such is the nazf that happens to the drinker of wine, so that what is in his stomach is drained out.

Likewise, in this world there is water, and in the Hereafter there is water; in this world there is milk, and in the Hereafter there is milk. But there is a vast difference between the water of the Hereafter and the water of this world, and between the milk of the Hereafter and the milk of this world. He, Exalted, says in explaining this: ﴿A description of Paradise which the God-conscious have been promised: in it are rivers of water unaltered, and rivers of milk whose taste does not change, and rivers of wine, delicious to the drinkers, and rivers of purified honey. And for them therein is every fruit…﴾ [Muhammad: 15].

Among the wonders of these rivers is that they are rivers without banks. They flow with what is in them of water, milk, wine or honey, yet some do not mix with others. This is a wonder that we place beneath "what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and has not occurred to the heart of any human."

So when the Truth, glorified is He, gives us the likeness of Paradise, He negates from it the harms present in its likeness in this world. The defect of water in this world is that it becomes stagnant (asin), meaning it changes and is no longer fit for drinking, whereas the water of the Hereafter is not stagnant, for it is flowing water in rivers, and the flow of water preserves it from becoming stagnant. Likewise with milk. And the description of honey as "purified" (musaffa) is because the honey of this world is not free of impurities.

As for the wine of the Hereafter, it is a delight to the drinkers, whose drinker savours it and sips it for the pleasure of its taste. But in this world, may God protect us, one pours it into his mouth all at once, because it is bitter in taste and foul in smell.

Among this also is His saying, in describing the bliss of Paradise: ﴿among lote-trees with thorns removed﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 28]. The lote-tree (sidr) is a tree well known to the Arab, and it was counted among their fruits and among the valuable things they possessed. But its defect is the thorns it has that harm the one who eats from it. So the Truth, glorified is He, negated this defect from the lote-trees of the Hereafter and said: ﴿among lote-trees with thorns removed﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 28], that is, cut down and stripped of thorns, not harming whoever takes its fruit.

So then: when the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, says in describing Paradise: ﴿For them are chambers, above which are built chambers, beneath which rivers flow — the promise of Allah; Allah does not fail in His promise﴾ [al-Zumar: 20], do not be amazed at how chambers are built above chambers while water flows beneath them; for God, the Exalted, has a particular engineering that falls under "what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and has not occurred to the heart of any human." These are things which the words of our language do not indicate.

But there are other things about which there is no disagreement, such as: ewers (abariq), cups (akwab), goblets (ka's), cushions (namariq), carpets (zarabi) and couches (ara'ik). These are among the blessings of God in Paradise, and they also exist in this world, but with a difference: these are the craft of humans for humans, and those are the craft of the Creator of humans for humans.

Therefore, when we went to (San Francisco) and saw there a luxurious hotel on a high hill, and found in it every means of comfort and luxury, everyone admired it. I said to them: "Are you amazed at this, which is the craft of humans for humans? Then what about the craft of the Truth for creation?"

This matter draws our attention and directs us to the bliss of the Hereafter. When you see the bliss of this world, and when you see a beautiful, dazzling thing, do not resent its owner nor envy him for it, but rather remember through it the bliss of God which He has prepared for His servants in the Hereafter. It is as if God, through the bliss of this world, makes us desirous of the bliss of the Hereafter.

As for what we have mentioned of the reward of the God-conscious, ﴿the promise of Allah; Allah does not fail in His promise﴾ [al-Zumar: 20]. Wa'd (promise) is the announcement of a pleasing, joyful thing before its time. Your informing of a happy matter before its time incites action toward reaching this promise. Its counterpart is wa'id (threat), which is the announcement of a painful thing before its time, its aim being warning, so that you do not fall into its causes. So the Truth, glorified is He, intends by promise and threat to make creation yearn for reward and warn them against punishment, and to make crimes and their penalties appear monstrous, so that we do not fall into them.

And Allah, glorified is He, does not fail in His promise, for His promise is true, because He, glorified is He, holds all the means of fulfilment, and there is no opponent who could turn Him away from fulfilling His promise. For the one who breaks a promise is subject to things that take him out of the capacity to fulfil it, and man is a son of changing circumstances, much given to fluctuation, so there befalls him what comes between him and the fulfilment of his promise. But the Truth, glorified is He, is the Truth that does not change, nothing is difficult for Him, and He, glorified is He, is the Capable who possesses absolute power.

And the Truth, glorified is He, shows us the fulfilment of His promise in this world, so that we may believe in His promise of the Hereafter. Allah promised the believers, saying: ﴿And indeed Our soldiers, they will be the victorious﴾ [al-Saffat: 173].

And He said: ﴿Allah will surely support those who support Him﴾ [al-Hajj: 40]. And Allah's promise to the believers was fulfilled, and they were victorious, even if they were persecuted at first. The fulfilment of this promise makes me trust in the promise of the Hereafter, which has not yet come in its time.

Therefore, our master 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, when he heard the saying of Allah: ﴿The multitude will be routed and they will turn their backs﴾ [al-Qamar: 45], said: "What multitude is this, when we are unable to protect ourselves?" Then when Badr came and the Muslims were victorious, he said: "Allah has spoken truly: ﴿The multitude will be routed and they will turn their backs﴾ [al-Qamar: 45]."

Thus the Truth, glorified is He, fulfils for us His promise that has come in its time, so that we may trust in the fulfilment of the promise that has not yet come in its time. Among this is His saying, concerning the disbelievers: ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outskirts? And Allah judges; there is no repeller of His judgement, and He is swift in reckoning﴾ [al-Ra'd: 41]. That is: O disbelievers of Quraysh, O you who oppose Muhammad and confront him, do you not see that your wide territory is shrinking, and Islam takes from it a portion every day? The meaning is: We diminish the land of disbelief and increase the land of Islam. And it is necessary that we say: Allah spoke truly in the first, and He must speak truly in the second, that is, on the Day of Resurrection.

Therefore the Truth, glorified is He, teaches us that when we promise something, we should accompany it with the will of God, saying: "If Allah wills." ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow," except [when adding], "If Allah wills"﴾ [al-Kahf: 23–24]. So that when it becomes impossible for you to fulfil it, you can say: "I willed, but Allah did not will." It is as if God bore it on behalf of His servants: the servant willed, but I did not will.

Thus God relieves you of embarrassment and protects you from being a liar. The Truth bears it on our behalf, just as He bore it on behalf of His Messenger, in His saying: ﴿We know indeed that what they say grieves you, but it is not you whom they deny; rather, the wrongdoers deny the signs of Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 33]. That is, their saying: "Sorcerer, soothsayer, liar, madman." ﴿For indeed they do not deny you﴾ [al-An'am: 33], because you are, in their eyes, truthful and trustworthy. ﴿But it is the wrongdoers who deny the signs of Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 33].

So He, glorified is He, placed it upon Himself, and He bore it on behalf of His Messenger.

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah 39, verse 21:

When God, exalted is He, speaks of His bounty, whether that bounty concerns the means of sustenance in this world or the provisions of delight in the Hereafter, He speaks of it as a sending down (inzal). The word anzala indicates the direction of height, and that this gift comes from above, even if it emerges from within the earth, as in His saying: ﴿And We sent down iron, wherein is mighty strength and benefits for mankind﴾ [al-Hadid: 25].

So the blessing comes from above and not from an equal. In the conduct of your life, when you face a matter beyond your capabilities and beyond what your mind can think through, you go to one who is higher than you in that field and whom you trust, and in his thought, to help you solve it. You do this willingly, because you have entrusted the matter to one whose abilities you trust.

So when God says "We sent down," it means: take My rulings as coming from above, and as the best for you, because they come from your Creator who knows what is good for you.

He, exalted is He, says here: ﴿Do you not see that God sends down water from the sky, and makes it flow as springs in the earth...﴾ [al-Zumar: 21]. The meaning of "from the sky" is: from the direction of the sky. Otherwise, the stores of water are in the earth, in the seas, and they are prepared chemically in such a way that they keep the water so that it does not change or become foul, and parasites do not live in it.

Thus you find the salt water in the seas is preserved by the proportion of salinity in the water; filth and carcasses are thrown into it, the waves cast them out, and the water remains in its wholesomeness. And from the water of the seas the process of evaporation takes place, which forms the clouds and the rain that waters humans, animals and plants.

Rainwater is the purest water that can be obtained. The process of evaporation is like the process of distillation of water that we carry out in laboratories to obtain pure water. Consider the cost of distilling a single bottle of water, so what of the rainwater that pours down from the sky?

Therefore, among the wisdom of the Creator, exalted is He, is that He made water three-quarters of the surface of the globe and made dry land a quarter. This is so that the area of evaporation is vast and the rain suffices the earth's need for sweet water. We have previously explained the difference between water that has depth and water that has a wide surface. Evaporation depends on the extent of the water's surface: the wider the surface, the greater the evaporation. We gave the example of a cup of water: if you leave it for a month and return to find it as it was, having lost only a little, but if you spill it on the floor of the room, it dries before you leave the room.

God, exalted is He, wishes the salt water to evaporate in order to be freed from its saltiness, and then to send down sweet water, pleasant to drinkers. This process of evaporation takes place, and we know nothing of it. It is one of God's signs and one of the greatest of His blessings upon us.

Water, when it descends from the sky, does not fall on every place; it falls on cold regions. The vapour gathered in the clouds, when it passes over a cold region, condenses anew, just as we condense distilled water. Where does the water that reaches us in the Nile fall? It falls on the Ethiopian highlands, and the rivers carry it to us, and part of it seeps into the earth, and God has made channels for it in the earth.

This is the meaning of ﴿and makes it flow as springs in the earth﴾ [al-Zumar: 21], meaning: He made for it special courses and channels, so that it does not mix with the salt water. Indeed, there may be, for example, a spring of sweet water welling up in the midst of salt water, yet it does not mix with it, as if the sweet water runs through special conduits, much like the arteries in the human body.

As for His saying here, ﴿Do you not see...﴾ [al-Zumar: 21], since it is a matter in which God bestows favour through sight, if you see it, know that it is a true statement; I see the rain falling from the sky. And if you do not see it, then believe what God has told you, just as you trust your eye in sight, because God's report to you is more truthful than the sight of your eyes.

Among this is His saying, addressing His Prophet ﷺ: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ [al-Fil: 1]. It is known that our master, the Messenger of God ﷺ, was born in the Year of the Elephant, meaning he did not witness that event. So the meaning of "Have you not seen" is: have you not known with knowledge from Me, which surpasses the knowledge of seeing with the eye.

Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿Then He brings forth thereby crops of varying colours﴾ [al-Zumar: 21]. The crop is sown in one soil, watered with one water, yet the fruits come out differing in colour, in taste and in their constituent elements.

When the scholars discussed this matter, they said: in plants there is a property called the property of selection (khasiyat al-intikhab), meaning that the plant absorbs through its roots the elements it needs from the earth. But if we take, for example, a vessel containing water and put several colours into it, then put into it narrow capillary tubes by which water rises upward through this property, we find these tubes absorb from the water in its generality and do not distinguish one colour from another.

But the plant's absorption of the elements it needs from the soil is not like that: the plant absorbs only the materials necessary and suitable to its nature. The capillary property in the roots absorbs with guidance, taking from the soil and leaving aside. The soil is one, the water is one, yet the flavours, shapes, colours and scents differ.

So this is not the selection that the scholars mean; rather it is a divine selection established by the nature which God deposited in the seed and the first grain of the plant. For example, you plant hot pepper beside sugarcane beside pomegranate, and you find this one hot, that one sweet, and that one bitter.

Then the plant passes to another stage, which the Almighty describes in His saying: ﴿Then it dries up, and you see it turning yellow; then He makes it crumbled debris﴾ [al-Zumar: 21]. The meaning of "yahij" is: it dries up and is broken and becomes crumbs. That is, it does not remain in its greenness and freshness. It is as if God made the plant a lesson for man: the plant is a living being like man, and man will pass through this stage, drying up and crumbling like the plant.

So God strikes a parable for us, so that we are not deceived by our selves when we find in them strength, or find in them intellect and thought, or authority and rank, or wealth. Your Lord says to you: look at your mother the earth, and at the crops that come out of it: where do they end? So it is with you; do not be deceived as long as you are of the people of change.

Therefore they say: do not be angry or grieved if things change for you, for you are of the people of change. And as long as you are of the people of change and have reached the peak of the mountain, what do you expect? Do you expect to settle upon it? How, when you are of the people of change? So you must descend. Hence, if blessing is complete, expect its passing, as the poet said:

When a thing is complete, its deficiency appears;
Watch for its decline once it is said to be complete.

So if you see yourself puffed up with knowledge, or strength, or any appearance of delight, know that tomorrow you will come to old age and to weakness; you will become like a child who crawls and needs one who supports and helps you, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And among you is he who is returned to the most abject age, so that he knows nothing after knowledge﴾ [al-Hajj: 5]. So understand this meaning well, in your mother the earth and in your own self.

﴿Indeed in that...﴾ [al-Zumar: 21]: that is, what you witness of what we have mentioned, ﴿is a reminder...﴾ [al-Zumar: 21], meaning: a reminder and a lesson, ﴿for those of understanding﴾ [al-Zumar: 21], for those with conscious and reflective minds.

The estimate here is: "Is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam [as one whose breast is constricted against it]?" So we must mention this opposite, because the two are not equal. "Woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah" shows that we have taken the constriction from the hardness, so the one whose breast is constricted against Islam has been constricted because of the hardness of his heart.

This is like His saying, "Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord [equal to the disbeliever]? Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know?" [al-Zumar: 9]. The meaning: Is this like one who does not worship devoutly? And it is for you to answer: Is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord, like one whose heart has hardened and whose breast has constricted against the religion of Allah and His guidance?

The meaning of "Allah has expanded his breast" is: He made the constriction spacious. You say to your companion, "Expand your breast," meaning: make it ample for discussing all matters. Among the meanings of breadth of the breast is that you do not occupy it with superstitions, nor crowd it with falsehood, so that it becomes familiar with you; then falsehood is expelled by truth, as we said in the matter of space (ḥayyiz).

A single space can hold only one thing. Water, for example, displaces air when you fill a bottle with water.

From the expansion of the breast is having justice in choosing when you choose between alternatives. You must purify your heart and remove from it everything that preoccupies it, then examine the matters presented to you. What you find suitable, you let into your heart so that it settles there until it becomes a firm belief that does not accept debate again. For Allah, may He be exalted, created for us senses that perceive: an eye that sees, an ear that hears, and a tongue that speaks.

Through these senses we take in information. Then we present it to the intellect so that it may choose from it and examine it. What it finds sound, it drops into the heart, and this is the belief that settles in the heart and does not float up to be examined anew.

Therefore beware of the rust (rān) that accumulates on the heart until it seals it, so that there is no room in it for the truth. The Prophet (ﷺ) points to this matter in the hadith of Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"Trials are presented to hearts like a mat, strand by strand (ʿūdan ʿūdan) — and in another narration, ʿawdhan ʿawdhan. Whatever heart absorbs them, a black spot is marked upon it; and whatever heart rejects them, a white spot is marked upon it, until there are two kinds of hearts: a white one like smooth stone, which no trial harms as long as the heavens and earth endure, and another black and clouded (murbaddan) — and this is the one about which Allah says: 'Nay! Rather, what they have been earning has covered over their hearts' [al-Mutaffifin: 14] — like an inverted cup (kūz mujkhiyan), upside down, that knows no good and denies no evil."

The trials here are the doubts (shubah) that come to people regarding religion. The Prophet (ﷺ) likens them to a mat woven strand beside strand, until it becomes like the mat we sit on. Or ʿawdhan means: we seek refuge with Allah from these trials. Or ʿawdan means: time after time.

So, if you want to examine the matter of faith, first expand your breast, and widen it by expelling from it the beliefs it holds. Therefore He, glorified is He, says: "Is one whose breast Allah has expanded for Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord?" Light has sources: either material light, like the sun, the moon and the stars, and the lights that man has recently discovered; or immaterial light, which is what is meant here, the light of values and method. "Upon a light from his Lord" means: the light of guidance that the Noble Qur'an intends in His saying: "In houses which Allah has permitted to be raised and in which His name is mentioned; glorifying Him therein in the mornings and evenings, men whom neither trade nor sale diverts from the remembrance of Allah" [al-Nur: 36-37]...

Allah has given you sensory light that helps you in the movement of life, so that a person sees where he places his feet, and does not break things nor is broken when he collides with them; and the immaterial light of values and of the spirit...

As for His saying, may He be glorified: "Woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah. They are in manifest error" — woe to them because the hardness of their hearts has stood between them and faith. Woe to them at the moment they recognise that they have a Lord whom they disbelieved in, and this reality that they long denied will confront them.

The Noble Qur'an has expressed this matter in His saying, may He be glorified: "The likeness of those who disbelieve in their Lord: their deeds are like ashes on which the wind blows violently on a stormy day; they have no power over anything of what they earned" [Ibrahim: 18].

The meaning: their deeds have come to nothing and their striving has been lost.

And He also said: "And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a low valley, which the thirsty man supposes to be water, until when he comes to it he finds it to be nothing; and he finds Allah with him, and He pays him his account in full. And Allah is swift in reckoning" [al-Nur: 39].

So woe to them at the moment they know that they disbelieved in Allah and their breasts were too constricted to make room for the light of faith. Their woe is present before the punishment reaches them.

As for His saying, "They are in manifest error": clear and evident. Error (ḍalāl) is failure to be guided along the path one travels, like a traveller in a desert who has lost the way. His straying begins with his deviation from the correct road even by a few centimetres, because it must end with him in vast expanses of error... So the meaning of "They are in manifest error" is: they will never be guided to anything at all.

Allah, exalted is He, says: "Since you follow what is best and choose it, I shall send down to you the best of statements." Indeed it is the best of statements, because it is the speech of Allah, and the speech of Allah is one of His attributes. It possesses absolute perfection, Allah has made it inimitable (mu'jiz), and He has Himself undertaken its preservation, not entrusting its preservation to the creation.

In human custom, a person preserves only that which serves as proof in his favour, and does not preserve that which is a proof against him. But as for the Truth, glory be to Him, He preserves the Qur'an, and it is a proof against His creation. Therefore everything that came in the Qur'an, Allah has guaranteed its occurrence, as He has informed us, because He is the one who sent it down and He is its preserver.

By "the best of statements" is meant the Noble Qur'an. The meaning of "mutashabihan" [al-Zumar: 23] is that part of it resembles another part in excellence, in eloquence, or in subject matter. So beware of saying: "This verse is more eloquent than that one," for every verse is eloquent in its subject...

As for His saying: "The skins of those who fear their Lord shiver from it..." This is the description of the servant who fears his Lord, watches over Him, and takes His seeing him into account, for he constantly presents his conduct before his Lord. If he sees in it any transgression, he returns to the words of Allah and recalls His threat, so a shivering arises in his skin out of fear of his Lord. This is when the skin dries and tightens, and a trembling occurs in the body from fear of punishment and fear of Allah's anger. Then he returns and recalls the mercy of his Lord which precedes His wrath, and His pardon which precedes His punishment, and so he returns to his first state: "Then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah."

Thus the believer combines fear and hope, and his heart is between these two matters. At the moment he recalls punishment for transgression, his skin shivers in fear; at the moment he recalls the mercy of his Lord, his skin softens and his heart becomes calm. And why not, when his Lord has said: "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins. Indeed, it is He who is the Forgiving, the Merciful" [al-Zumar: 53].

(That is) and this is what happens to the believer. "This is the guidance of Allah; He guides thereby whom He wills, and whoever Allah sends astray, for him there is no guide" [al-Zumar: 23]. Many have paused at this verse, saying: since it is Allah who misguides, why does He punish the misguided? The meaning of "whoever Allah sends astray" is: he knows his own error, and knows that he will not hear His speech nor follow His way. Allah created him choosing: if he wills, he believes, and if he wills, he disbelieves. Therefore the disbeliever did not disbelieve against Allah's will; rather, has Allah been pleased with that from him?

As for His saying: "for him there is no guide," it means: beware of presuming to correct Allah with human judgments that the minds of those who disdain to take from Allah devise for you. Since Allah has spoken, it is not right for us to presume to correct Him, glory be to Him, for it is impossible for us to bring guidance better than the guidance of Allah.

**Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66)**, on surah 39, verse 24:

The interrogative in *afa-man* (أفمن) is like its counterpart in His saying ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has opened to Islam...﴾ [Az-Zumar: 22]. Therefore we must supply the opposite here. The meaning is: ﴿Is one who shields with his face from the terrible torment on the Day of Resurrection [like one who is not tormented]?﴾ We may also elevate the matter and say: [like one who is given bliss]? The choice is yours to judge.

The meaning of *su'a al-adhab* (سُوءَ الْعَذَابِ) is: the severe, evil torment. Consider ﴿yattaqi bi-wajhihi su'a al-adhab﴾ ("shields with his face from the evil torment"). It is well known that the face is the most noble of the human body's members, and by it the features of creation are distinguished. Therefore He says: ﴿Their mark is on their faces﴾ [Al-Fath: 29].

Were it not for the features of faces, bodies would be equal and resemble one another. Thus a person takes care of his face, defends it and protects it first. Let us illustrate this with a man walking along the road when a car passes by and splashes mud on him and his clothes. By Allah, what is the first thing he is eager to clean and rid of harm? He wipes his face first, then turns to his clothes, because the face is the noblest, most prominent and most honoured of the members, and it is the most protected before all the other limbs.

So what of a torment from which a person finds nothing to shield himself except his face? Yes, he shields himself from the torment with his face, because his hands are chained and his feet are shackled. He has no escape and no deliverance, so he can do nothing but ward off the torment from himself with the dearest thing he possesses and the most noble of his members, which is the face.

﴿And it will be said to the wrongdoers: Taste what you used to earn.﴾ His saying about the torment, *dhuqu* (ذُوقُوا, "taste"), is a mockery of them. He chose *al-dhawq* (الذوق, "tasting"), which is one of the members that perform a function in the human body, like the eye and the ear. He specifically chose tasting because *al-dhawq* is the sense that is constantly with a person, and by it life is sustained, since through tasting we take in food and drink, enjoy them, and find in them a pleasure that surpasses other pleasures.

As for the eye and the ear, for example, you may see or hear what does not please you. But in tasting you choose what pleases you and find pleasure in it. Here, the Truth, glory be to Him, wants to generalise tasting throughout the whole body, so the entire body tastes the torment.

We have said that the tongue is the organ of tasting, with its stages and what surrounds it; it tastes and distinguishes flavours. When food passes beyond this region, a person no longer perceives any flavour in it. This is why we see medicine makers coat bitter medicine with an agreeable, acceptable substance that helps the medicine pass through the region of tasting without our sensing its bitterness.

If you look at all the members, you will find that they relate to others: I hear others, I see others, I touch others or a part of myself. But tasting belongs to the person himself, so no one tastes for another. Therefore Allah, glory be to Him, chose this member to show the intensity and pain of the torment: ﴿dhuqu﴾ ("taste"), and in another place ﴿dhuq﴾ (ذُقْ, "taste," singular). There is no seeing, no hearing, no smelling, no touching, but only tasting, which belongs to its owner, as if each of them has a flavour suited to his torment.

If tasting has a specific region, namely the tongue with its stages and what surrounds it, then here Allah intended tasting to be general and all-encompassing: not in the region of tasting, but the whole body tastes the torment. The proof is His saying: ﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins that they may taste the torment﴾ [An-Nisa: 56]. Thus tasting here exceeds the region of taste to the whole body.

When we consider, by way of reflection, His saying about the town that was secure and at peace but denied the blessings of Allah, Allah said of it: ﴿So Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear﴾ [An-Nahl: 112]. It is as if the tasting clothes them and encompasses them from every side...

His saying: ﴿what you used to earn (ma kuntum taksibun)﴾. The root *k-s-b* (كسب) in the Noble Qur'an comes, as we have said, in two forms: *kasaba* (كسب) and *iktasaba* (اكتسب). The Truth, glory be to Him, has made clear the object of each of them in His saying: ﴿For it is what it earned, and against it is what it has acquired﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 286]. So *kasaba* is for good and *iktasaba* is for evil, because *kasaba* is on the pattern *fa'ala*, and good comes from its doer naturally, with no effort or artificiality in it. As for *iktasaba*, it is on the pattern *ifta'ala*, which includes artifice (*ifti'al*, "contrivance"), and contrivance is only found in evil. Good does not require you to resort to tricks and contrivance; it comes naturally, unlike evil.

We have explained this matter with the example of a man sitting with his wife and daughters, looking at their beauty in a natural way, with no caution about anything and no fear of anything. But if he wants to look at a beautiful woman in the street, for example, he sneaks and schemes for it. This is *ifti'al* (contrivance).

Yet the Noble Qur'an departs from this rule in some places. Among them is this verse: ﴿It will be said to the wrongdoers: Taste what you used to earn (taksibun)﴾, and it does not say *taktasibun*. So it used *kasaba* for evil. In another place too He says: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed, and his sin has encompassed him, those are the companions of the Fire, in it they will abide forever﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 81].

Why did the Qur'an turn from *iktasaba* to *kasaba*? They said: because a person, may Allah protect us, may become accustomed to sin and familiar with disobedience until it becomes a habit that he does naturally, delights in, and feels at ease with as though it were obedience. This is what we call (*faqid*). Because he has become familiar with it and accustomed to it, and even rejoices in it, the Qur'an expressed it with *kasaba*, which is used for good, and transferred the acquisition to the place of earning.

Therefore the Qur'an distinguishes between one who contrives sin, intends it and seeks it out, and one upon whom sin falls without his preparing for it. Consider the saying of Allah: ﴿Repentance with Allah is only for those who do evil in ignorance and then repent soon after. Those are the ones to whom Allah turns in forgiveness, and Allah is ever Knowing and Wise. And repentance is not for those who keep doing evil deeds until, when death comes to one of them, he says: "Indeed, I have repented now," nor for those who die while they are disbelievers. For those, We have prepared a painful punishment﴾ [An-Nisa: 17–18].

The meaning of *bi-jahalah* (بِجَهَالَةٍ, "in ignorance") is: without intending it, without arrangement, and without seeking it out. If evil happens from them, they do not rejoice in it; rather they grieve and regret. As for the other type, he commits evil deeds deliberately and does not care; perhaps he rejoices in them and even openly displays them.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 39, verses 25–26:

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Those before them denied, so the punishment came upon them﴾ [al-Zumar: 25], meaning: from the earlier nations. ﴿So the punishment came upon them﴾ [al-Zumar: 25], meaning: the punishment of this world, through their defeat and the victory of the religion which they were fighting and opposing. This also is what befell the disbelievers, when God granted victory to Islam and made its principles and matters prevail over the principles of disbelief. This in itself is a kind of punishment in this world. Then, when they return to God in the Hereafter, there will be another punishment, more severe and more painful.

Therefore: they resemble those deniers who came before them. For this reason He said elsewhere: ﴿Like the custom of¦﴾ [Al 'Imran: 11].

Accordingly, His saying (kadhdhaba, "denied") here and (ka-da'b, "like the custom of") there reveals to us a psychological matter in the Noble Qur'an: that the memorisers of the Qur'an should not be from among the scholars, especially the scholars of language and eloquence. This is because the scholar, when he stops at a word in the Qur'an, is able to alter it and complete his recitation. He says, for example: ﴿O you who believe, if a dissolute person brings you news, then verify﴾ [al-Hujurat: 6]; he says: "then be firm" or "then investigate," and the meaning may stand. But the Truthful One (al-Haqq, subhanahu) wants a specific word which we may not go beyond to another. As for the one who has specialised in memorising the Qur'an and does not have this faculty of alteration, if he forgets or stops at a word, he stops at it (with the four), meaning he cannot alter it. This is what is required of the guardians of God's speech, and this is among the greatness of the Qur'an.

Therefore we have said: the perfection of the Qur'an does not transfer to anything else. How? For example, if we wanted a person to refine his style and strengthen it in composed prose, we would advise him to read the literary books of al-Manfaluti, al-Rafi'i and others. When he increases these readings, we notice an improvement in his style and expression.

Then, the memoriser of the Qur'an who has mastered it, even if he has memorised it ten ways and is told "write a letter," you will find he cannot write it eloquently at all. Why? Because the perfection of the Qur'an does not extend to anything else; rather, human eloquence extends to humans.

His saying: ﴿from where they did not perceive﴾ [al-Zumar: 25], meaning: from where they did not estimate or expect, as the punishment overtakes them that was not in their reckoning and had never occurred to them, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and found God with him, and He paid him his account in full, and God is swift at reckoning﴾ [al-Nur: 39]. Meaning: he was confronted with it, confronted with a reckoning other than what he was expecting, because he had denied in this world the Resurrection and the Reckoning, and now the reckoning he denied confronts him.

Then He, glorified is He, says: ﴿So God made them taste disgrace in the life of this world...﴾ [al-Zumar: 26]. Here the tasting of the physical is transferred to tastes of the moral. Disgrace and humiliation are a kind of punishment, and they carry a pain that exceeds physical pain. Some people are not hurt by a beating, but are hurt by a cutting word that scratches their honour and dignity.

But why did God make them taste disgrace in this world before the punishment of the Hereafter? He made them taste disgrace because they were arrogant towards the truth and tyrannical, and they came with all their force and multitude to Badr to fight Islam, and they thought that they were the champions and that the round was theirs. The intended ones, then, are the chiefs of Quraysh and the heads of disbelief, such as 'Utba, Shayba, al-Walid and others. They came with numbers and equipment, while the Muslims had not gone out to fight but had gone out for the caravan. Nevertheless, God honoured His army and disgraced His enemy: some of them were killed, some were taken captive, and they were humiliated. And the disgrace for these was more painful than killing.

Accordingly: they had disgrace in this world, but in the Hereafter there is a punishment: ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew﴾ [al-Zumar: 26]. Yes, the punishment of the Hereafter is greater than the disgrace of this world and more severe, ﴿if they only knew﴾ [al-Zumar: 26], because those who knew this truth desisted and believed, whereas these persisted, were obstinate, and denied.
