Therefore, those who want to reconcile the reports said: perhaps when Wahshi killed Hamzah and remembered his station in Islam, and that he was the Lion of God, he despaired of God's mercy, and this despair might have led him to more evil and wickedness. A righteous man met him and said to him: "Do not despair of the mercy of God, for God the Exalted has said: ﴿Say: O My servants who have been extravagant against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God. Indeed, God forgives all sins. Indeed, it is He who is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ [al-Zumar 39:53]."

When Wahshi heard these words, he embraced Islam. Nothing prevented him from Islam except fear of what he had done. But if the matter of forgiveness is of this kind, why did he not embrace Islam, when his Lord had guaranteed him forgiveness? So: the verse preceded this story, and it was not revealed specifically about him; rather, it was revealed before him, but it was recited to him and read to him, and so it was the cause of his embracing Islam.

And the phrase ﴿Indeed, it is He who is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ [al-Zumar 39:53] restricted forgiveness and mercy to Him (exalted is He), because every sin is a right of God the Exalted, and since sin is a right of God, He alone has the authority to forgive it and to show mercy to its doer. He (exalted is He) also has the right to take to account and to punish, because He (exalted is He) has absolute power, and there is no other god with Him who could object to Him.

This meaning is clear in the story of our master Jesus, peace be upon him, in His saying: ﴿And when God says: "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides God?'" He will say: "Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to. If I had said it, You would have known it. You know what is within myself, and I do not know what is within Yourself. Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen. I did not say to them except what You commanded me: 'Worship God, my Lord and your Lord.' And I was a witness over them as long as I remained among them; but when You took me up, You were the Watcher over them, and You are Witness over all things. If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise.﴾ [al-Maʾidah 5:116-118].

We note here, in the conclusion of this verse, that He did not say "Indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful," which would have been the fitting ending for forgiveness, but said: ﴿Indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ [al-Maʾidah 5:118]. His saying "the Exalted in Might, the Wise" indicates that Jesus, peace be upon him, held that they must be requited for this slander, but God the Exalted has absolute power to forgive or to punish. Had He had a partner in this matter, He would not have said that. Rather, He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise, whom no one can call to account for what He does. He is the One who forgives them, not because He is Forgiving and Merciful, but because they deserve punishment, and if God forgives them, it is because He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.

Repentance and turning back (al-Inabah) is tawbah and returning to the domain of faith in God, one God with no partner. Islam is that you carry out what God requires of you in commands and prohibitions: "do" and "do not."

But does inabah mean that they were with God, then turned away from Him to disbelief, so that they are asked to return to the domain of faith once more? We say: no. Rather, the meaning of inabah here is a return to the first covenant that God took from His servants while they were in the realm of atoms (alam al-dharr), when they were in the loins of Adam (peace be upon him). This is the covenant about which God said: ﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves, "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes, we have testified." [This] lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were of this unaware"﴾ [al-A'raf: 172].

So the meaning of ﴿And turn back to your Lord﴾ [al-Zumar: 54] is: return to your natural faith (al-iman al-fitri), the faith by which the covenant was taken from you. This natural faith is what accompanies a person, so that his conscience awakens after sin and he repents, or after disbelief and he believes. This natural faith, settled in the depths of the human soul, is what alerts it if it becomes heedless. This faith is what alerted Khalid ibn al-Walid, Amr ibn al-As and others, so they believed when they returned to the first covenant and the natural faith.

﴿Before the punishment comes upon you, and then you will not be helped﴾ [al-Zumar: 54]. What is the meaning of help (al-nusrah) here, when the discussion is about the Hereafter? It means: the people of falsehood do not support one another, and none of them defends another, neither the follower nor the one followed, as He, glorified is He, said in another place: ﴿What is [wrong] with you that you do not help one another? Rather, they are today submissive. And they will approach each other, questioning one another. They will say, "Indeed, you used to come to us from the right." They will say, "No, you were not believers. And we did not have over you any authority; rather, you were a transgressing people."﴾ [al-Saffat: 25-30].

Yes, they do not help one another, because the situation here is one of hostility and blame, where each of them throws the responsibility onto the other and each disowns the other. Therefore He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Intimate friends that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 67].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 39, verse 55:

The word (aḥsan) (ahsan, "better/best") is an elative (ism tafḍīl) that indicates intensification, and from it we understand that what is less in goodness is (also) good. We say: "This is good, and this is better than it." The command here is to follow the best (al-aḥsan). For example, Allah, glorified is He, sends down rulings that satisfy the human soul, so that it does not become filled with rage and hatred toward people. So He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾ [An-Nahl: 126].

That is: beware of exceeding the like-for-like if you wish to punish. If you are able to restrict yourself to this equivalence without exceeding it, that is good; but the better than it is that you pardon, as He, glorified is He, said in another verse: ﴿But whoever is pardoned by his brother [something], then [the decision] should be followed with fairness and payment to him with good conduct..﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 178].

And He said: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives – indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination﴾ [Ash-Shura: 43].

This is the best (al-aḥsan). And from this is His saying, exalted is He, regarding the matter of adoption: ﴿Call them by [the names of] their fathers; that is more just in the sight of Allah﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 5]. You know the story of the adoption of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of Zayd ibn Harithah, and that Zayd was given the choice between his family and the Messenger of Allah, and he chose to remain with the Messenger of Allah, and said: "I would never choose anyone over the Messenger of Allah." Therefore the Messenger of Allah rewarded him and attributed him to himself, saying: "Zayd ibn Muhammad."

When Allah, glorified is He, wished to prohibit adoption and sent down ﴿Call them by [the names of] their fathers﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 5], He did justice to our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and made his action good. But the will of Allah is better, and the action of the Messenger of Allah was (a matter of) qist (equity), while the choice of Allah is more just: ﴿that is more just in the sight of Allah﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 5]. And the wisdom behind ﴿Call them by [the names of] their fathers﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 5] is so that you do not waste the cause of existence, which is the father, because wasting the immediate cause of existence, which is the father, emboldens you to deny the highest cause of existence, glorified is He.

Or we may say: the meaning of ﴿And follow the best of what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [Az-Zumar: 55] is that the Qur'an was revealed when there were two religions among the people: Judaism, whose scripture is the Torah, and Christianity, whose scripture is the Gospel. When these books and others were revealed, there were people who believed in them, and others who disbelieved and associated partners (with Allah), and among them were even atheists.

So the command in (wa-ittabi'u, "and follow") is addressed to all: that is, O you who believed in Moses, and O you who believed in Jesus. This religion was good in its time; but now Islam has come, the seal of religions, dominant over all religions, and it has become the best, which it is obligatory upon you to follow.

Sometimes the elative gives the actual state (of comparison) but does not look at its opposite, which is the worst, rather it looks at the one equal in the attribute but with less of it; except in one thing we have noticed concerning Allah, the Exalted. Among His names is al-Kabir (the Great), and not al-Akbar (the Greatest), although by the rule it should have been al-Akbar, since it is an intensive form of al-Kabir. So why?

We say: the word Akbar (al-Akbar) has come as an attribute of Allah, glorified is He, which we hear every day in every adhan and every iqamah for prayer. And prayer is a worship with its own distinction and rank in the religion: it is the worship repeated five times each day, the worship that never falls from the believer as long as there is a breath that comes and goes, and the worship that was not legislated by revelation like the other acts of worship, but was legislated directly during the Mi'raj journey. When we call to this worship we say: Allahu Akbar, and do not say: Allahu Kabir.

Here is the place of greatness, although akbar is more eloquent in meaning than kabir, because the obligations from Allah, glorified is He, do not only want from you prayer, fasting, hajj, etc., but want from you that you perform every beneficial movement in life that aids religiosity. Therefore the scholars said in the legal principles: "What the obligation cannot be completed without is itself obligatory."

Consider, for example, the obligation of prayer: how many actions are necessary for this obligation to be performed? Take for example covering the awrah, which is an obligation without which prayer is not complete. In order to cover your awrah to pray, you need a garment to wear. How is this garment available to you? It requires a tailor who sews it, and a retail merchant from whom you buy the cloth, then a wholesale merchant, then the factory of weaving, spinning, dyeing and ginning, then the farmer who plants the cotton and gathers it.

All this process requires equipment, machines, tools and workers. Likewise the case with food, which you cannot do without in order to be strong enough to perform the obligations; all this movement is for your sake, serving you and aiding you. So these worldly works, without which religion is not established, are obligatory and not to be belittled; rather they must be preserved and held sacred, because they hold the rank of obligation.

And when your Lord takes you from these works to prayer, for example, He does not take you from a trivial, insignificant work of no value; rather He takes you from a work which in itself is worship. Therefore He made it (the work) great; but the One who calls you to prayer is greater than all this. Therefore Allah, glorified is He, did not call the believer to a prayer (by name of a day) except in the Friday prayer, where He said, glorified is He: ﴿O you who have believed, when the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday, then proceed to the remembrance of Allah and leave trade..﴾ [Al-Jumu'ah: 9].

He specified trade above all other works, because it is the fruit of the other works of commerce, agriculture and industry, and a person is more eager for selling than for buying, because selling is the quick-profit transaction; therefore you find a person eager to sell, unlike the buyer. For example, when the buyer does not find the commodity he wants, he says ("blessing, O gatherer"), because he will pay from his pocket; but the seller takes and profits.

So when the prayer ends, your Lord returns you to the work from which He summoned you and sends you back to your worldly life: ﴿And when the prayer has been concluded, disperse within the land and seek from the bounty of Allah..﴾ [Al-Jumu'ah: 10].

Therefore: do not belittle the work of this world, nor think it far from religion; rather it is part of it, and what the religious obligation cannot be completed without is itself obligatory. Whoever disobeys in this is like whoever disobeys in that. So when we say in the call to prayer, Allahu Akbar, remember that whatever else is great should not be belittled; but the One who gives you strength is greater than this greatness, so do not preoccupy yourself with the great to the neglect of the Greatest.

Now the wisdom becomes clear in that Allah, exalted is He, named Himself al-Kabir and not al-Akbar. When we say "Allah is Kabir," this means that everything other than Him is small; but if we say Akbar, then everything other than Him is (merely) great.

Therefore: when you stand before His rulings, between (ḥasan, "good") and (aḥsan, "better"), follow the best of what has been revealed: ﴿And follow the best of what has been revealed to you from your Lord..﴾ [Az-Zumar: 55].

And the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿before the punishment comes upon you suddenly while you do not perceive﴾ [Az-Zumar: 55].

The word (baghtah) means suddenly, and punishment does not surprise except the heedless, carefree one who lives and does not have this matter in mind; for if it were in his mind, he would have guarded against it and avoided its causes, and when it comes it will not be sudden.

But how does punishment surprise him? We say: what is the difference between a person living his life in this world and encountering punishment? The difference between them is that he dies. The moment he dies and his soul departs, he moves from the expanse of this world to the punishment of the Hereafter, if he is among the people of punishment, and we seek refuge in Allah.

It is well known that the departure of the soul has no appointed time and no one knows it, for the soul may at any moment enter and not exit. This matter ought to be in the mind of the believer; he should never neglect it.

This is a model of the soul when it grieves and blames itself: "Why did you bring yourself to this position? We asked you to turn in repentance to God, to submit to His rulings, and to follow the best of what was sent down to you, so that you would lift from yourself distress and spare yourself blame. You should not have stood in this position, but you did not respond."

The phrase ﴿Yā ḥasratā﴾ [al-Zumar: 56] is a form of address (nidā'). What is it that the servant addresses? He addresses regret, grief and sorrow, saying: "O my regret, come forth, come to me, for this is your time." He grieves over himself after the opportunity has passed. It is known in the nidā' that one only calls upon what is beneficial, but the situation here is one of grief and remorse. The word ḥasrah here is attached to the first-person pronoun (yā' al-mutakallim), and the alif is for lengthening (al-iṭlāq).

The meaning of ﴿ʿalā mā farraṭtu fī janbi Allāh﴾ [al-Zumar: 56] is: "over what I neglected in the right of God and in obedience to Him." Al-tafrīṭ (neglect) is the failure to attend to what should have come first, because once an opportunity is lost, it cannot be compensated.

So: you grieve over yourself and blame yourself, because you did not seize the opportunity, you neglected it until it slipped away, and it cannot be made up. There remains for you only grief and biting the fingers of regret. It is as though the two commands that preceded this verse, namely ﴿And turn in repentance to your Lord and submit to Him﴾ [al-Zumar: 54], and ﴿And follow the best of what was sent down to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Zumar: 55], were to be acted upon so that they would protect themselves from saying, at the moment they see the punishment, ﴿Yā ḥasratā ʿalā mā farraṭtu fī janbi Allāh﴾ [al-Zumar: 56]. God's mercy and gentleness toward His servants do not wish that they say this word; God does not want His servant to stand in the position of grief, nor does He approve of it for him. Thus when He says to us: ﴿Do not despair of the mercy of God﴾, and ﴿turn in repentance﴾, and ﴿submit﴾, and ﴿seek the best of what has been sent down to you﴾, He wishes to alert the heedless, warn the one who contemplates disbelief, and remind him of the consequences and of what will come from him when he sees the punishment of regret.

Ḥasrah (regret) is sorrow and remorse over a good that has passed and cannot be recovered. The disbeliever does not grieve with a single grief but with many grieves that cling to him: whenever he sees the punishment descending upon him he grieves, whenever he sees the believers in bliss he grieves, and whenever he recalls his worldly life he grieves.

As for God's saying: ﴿And indeed, I was among the mockers﴾ [al-Zumar: 56], it means: the matter did not end at the limit of neglect and shortcoming in the right of God; rather it extended to mocking those who stand in the right of God. So the sin is doubled. We have already mentioned an example of the mockery of the people of falsehood toward the people of truth and their derision of them in His saying in Surat al-Muṭaffifīn: ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed. And when they passed by them, they would exchange winks. And when they returned to their people, they returned jesting. And when they saw them, they said, "Indeed, these are misguided." But they had not been sent as guardians over them. So today, those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers, upon couches, observing. Have the disbelievers been recompensed for what they used to do?﴾ [al-Muṭaffifīn: 29–36]...

Commentary on the words of God Most High: "Or [lest] it say, when it sees the punishment, 'If only I had a return [to the world], so that I might be among the good-doers'" (39:57–58).

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿أَوْ تَقُولَ﴾ [Az-Zumar: 57], i.e., the soul, ﴿لَوْ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ هَدَانِي﴾ [Az-Zumar: 57], i.e., in the worldly life, ﴿لَكُـنتُ مِنَ ٱلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾ [Az-Zumar: 57]. And this is strange: it is strange that you would lie even in the Hereafter, because the meaning of ﴿لَوْ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ هَدَانِي﴾ [Az-Zumar: 57] is that He, glorified is He, did not guide you, and this is a lie.

A person says in defending himself: "My not being in the ranks of the God-fearing is because God did not guide me." This is a lie, because God did guide you, showed you the way, directed you to the path of good, and made clear to you the lawful and the unlawful; but you did not follow His guidance and did not walk in His method. ﴿أَوْ تَقُولَ حِينَ تَرَى ٱلْعَذَابَ لَوْ أَنَّ لِي كَـرَّةً﴾ [Az-Zumar: 58], meaning: a return and a coming back to the world once more.

As He, glorified is He, said in another place: ﴿حَتَّىٰ إِذَا جَآءَ أَحَدَهُمُ ٱلْمَوْتُ قَالَ رَبِّ ٱرْجِعُونِ﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 99] ("until, when death comes to one of them, he says: My Lord, send me back"). All these are false wishes, so do not believe them; were they returned, they would revert to what they were, and just as they lied in the first [statement], ﴿لَوْ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ هَدَانِي﴾ [Az-Zumar: 57], they lied in ﴿فَأَكُونَ مِنَ ٱلْمُحْسِنِينَ﴾ [Az-Zumar: 58].

Lying may be conceived of in a person in the world, but it is strange that he should lie in the Hereafter, while standing before his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic. Therefore the Truth will say after it: ﴿وَيَوْمَ ٱلْقِيَامَةِ تَرَى ٱلَّذِينَ كَذَبُواْ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ وُجُوهُهُم مُّسْوَدَّةٌ﴾ [Az-Zumar: 60] ("And on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied against God, their faces blackened").

It appears that lying (clung) to them, and they became accustomed to it, to the point that they carried it with them into the Hereafter.

Then the Truth responds to this lie, saying, Exalted is He:

﴿بَلَىٰ قَدْ جَآءَتْكَ آيَاتِي فَكَذَّبْتَ بِهَا وَٱسْتَكْبَرْتَ...﴾ ("Yes! My signs did come to you, but you denied them and were arrogant...").

Commentary on the words of God Most High: "Or [lest] it say, when it sees the punishment, 'If only I had a return [to the world], so that I might be among the good-doers'" (39:57–58).

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿أَوْ تَقُولَ﴾ [Az-Zumar: 57], i.e., the soul, ﴿لَوْ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ هَدَانِي﴾ [Az-Zumar: 57], i.e., in the worldly life, ﴿لَكُـنتُ مِنَ ٱلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾ [Az-Zumar: 57]. And this is strange: it is strange that you would lie even in the Hereafter, because the meaning of ﴿لَوْ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ هَدَانِي﴾ [Az-Zumar: 57] is that He, glorified is He, did not guide you, and this is a lie.
